messages.subject_clean: with facet_grid locking scales by column and row but not both.
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggploters,
I'm struggling with an issue that someone may have already addressed.
I'm happy to come up with a toy example if needed, but for now I'll
through it out there see if anyone knows the answer.

I have a data frame that is the result of simulations.  I have 3
variables estimated in 3 different circumstances/methods.  I would
like to have a plot that shows with facet_grid(variable ~ situation)
or situation~variable the density of each variable under each of the
situations.  the problem is that the scales are different for the
variables and I get useless plots because the x and y scales are
locked to a global scale.  is there a way to lock the range for each
column/row separately. so that each variable only sees the relevant
area for that variable?

Thanks,
Andrew Redd

messages.subject_clean: qplot error: cannot coerce class '"times"' into a data.frame
messages.body_plain:
I'm going through Hadley Wickham's ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis and am trying to apply the examples to my own data after running through the example data.

I have a data frame dallas with three columns. The column offense_time contains times objects from the chron library.

Behind the scenes, the values are stored as floating point numbers between 0 and 1, where 0 = 0:00 midnight, 0.5 = 12 noon, and 0.999988425...  = 23:59:59.

For example, if I do this:

> d <- times("13:02:00")
> fix(d)

I get this:
structure(0.543055555555556, format = "h:m:s", class = "times")

I get this error:

> qplot(dallas$offense_time,data=dallas,geom="histogram",binwidth=1)
Error in as.data.frame.default(x[[i]], optional = TRUE) :
  cannot coerce class '"times"' into a data.frame

I tried to do some searching. I found some posts on this forum that are kind of related to this but don't answer the direct problem.

Is it possible to use items of class times with ggplot2?

Aren

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to convert an existing xyplot to ggplot2 (which I have never
used before) and would appreciate some tips.

I have a number of pass/fail observations each day and I want to plot
the proportion of passes for each date.  The qplot at the end is
tantalisingly close to what I want but I couldn't get near to this as a
scatter plot.

I would like the y scale min to float (rather than hard wired to zero)
because my actual dataset has pass rates close to one.

There are a couple of other things I would like on the plot which I have
left out of the example for clarity, including a mean line and an
arbitrary horizontal line.  Showing the pass rate as a percentage would
be nice.

# Setup data frame
date <- as.POSIXct(c(rep('2012-01-01', 20), rep('2012-01-02', 21),
                 rep('2012-01-03', 19), rep('2012-01-04', 20)))
verdict <- factor(rbinom(length(date), 1, 0.2), labels=c("PASS", "FAIL"))
df <- data.frame(date, verdict)

# my current version looks something like this
x <- prop.table(xtabs(~ date + verdict, data=df), 1)
print(xyplot(100*x[,1] ~ as.POSIXct(rownames(x)), type="b",
                 prepanel=function(x, y, ...) {
                     list(xlim=c(min(x) - 1, max(x) + 1),
                                 ylim=c(min(y) - 1, 100))
                 }))

# Close but no cigar
qplot(date, data=df, geom="bar", fill=verdict, position="fill")

messages.subject: Re: convert existing xyplot to ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: convert existing xyplot to ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

There are several things going on here, not all of which have to do
with ggplot2 directly but which you need to know in order to work with
it. ggplot2 can be a little intimidating at first, especially when you
start trying things on your own.

The first thing you need to know is that ggplot2 generally prefers
data frames as input; your life will be simpler if you heed that
advice. Your input object x is an object of class 'xtabs':

> str(x)
 xtabs [1:4, 1:2] 0.75 0.762 0.842 1 0.25 ...
 - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "xtabs" "table"
 - attr(*, "call")= language xtabs(formula = ~date + verdict, data = df)
 - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
  ..$ date   : chr [1:4] "2012-01-01" "2012-01-02" "2012-01-03" "2012-01-04"
  ..$ verdict: chr [1:2] "PASS" "FAIL"

If you use x as the input data object in qplot(), this happens:

> qplot(date, verdict, data = x)
Error: ggplot2 doesn't know how to deal with data of class xtabstable

...so you need to convert x to a data frame:

x <- as.data.frame(x)
### subselect the PASS values:
xp <- subset(x, verdict == 'PASS')

There is still a problem: when R converts an xtabs object to a data
frame, it coerces character objects to factor by default:

> str(xp)
'data.frame':   4 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ date   : Factor w/ 4 levels "2012-01-01","2012-01-02",..: 1 2 3 4
 $ verdict: Factor w/ 2 levels "PASS","FAIL": 1 1 1 1
 $ Freq   : num  0.7 0.857 0.842 0.8

One way to get around that is to use the stringsAsFactors = FALSE
argument in as.data.frame():

> x <- as.data.frame(x, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
> str(x)
'data.frame':   8 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ date   : chr  "2012-01-01" "2012-01-02" "2012-01-03" "2012-01-04" ...
 $ verdict: chr  "PASS" "PASS" "PASS" "PASS" ...
 $ Freq   : num  0.7 0.857 0.842 0.8 0.3 ...

You want to plot PASS verdict proportions over time, so we need to
subset the data frame and convert the date from character to Date
format, since dates have a linear ordering:

x$date <- as.Date(x$date)
xp <- subset(x, verdict == 'PASS')

Now we can do the plots. Wrinkle: a new version of ggplot2 is about to
be released and some of the documented code has been changed. I'll
show you how to do the plot both in the current 0.8.9 version and the
upcoming 0.9.0 version, and use both the qplot() and ggplot() forms of
producing the plot.

#### Current version 0.8.9:

ggplot(xp, aes(x = date, y = Freq)) +
    geom_point(colour = 'blue', size = 2.5) +
    geom_line(colour = 'blue', size = 1) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, colour = 'gray50') +
    scale_x_date(format = '%Y-%m-%d') +
    ylab('Pass proportion')

qplot(date, Freq, data = xp, geom = c('point', 'line')) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, colour = 'gray50') +
    scale_x_date(format = '%Y-%m-%d') +
    ylab('Pass proportion')

# to match the ggplot() output:
qplot(date, Freq, data = xp) +
      geom_point(colour = 'blue', size = 2.5) +
     geom_line(colour = 'blue', size = 1) +
     geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, colour = 'gray50') +
     scale_x_date(format = '%Y-%m-%d') +
     ylab('Pass proportion')

### version 0.9.0
ggplot(xp, aes(x = date, y = Freq)) +
    geom_point(colour = 'blue', size = 2.5) +
    geom_line(colour = 'blue', size = 1) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, colour = 'gray50') +
    scale_x_date(labels = date_format('%Y-%m-%d')) +
    ylab('Pass proportion')

qplot(date, Freq, data = xp, geom = c('point', 'line')) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, colour = 'gray50') +
    scale_x_date(labels = date_format('%Y-%m-%d')) +
    ylab('Pass proportion')

These work because the variable on the x-axis is a date, so
geom_line() and geom_path() will play nice. Had you left date as a
character or factor variable, the line would not have been rendered
unless you added a group = argument. The point is that you have to pay
attention to what you have in the input data object, which is why I
exhibited the output of str() several times.

geom_hline() is what you use to get a horizontal line. The key
argument is yintercept = ; in this case I chose 0.95. You can modify
the characteristics of the line; see
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_hline.html for further details and
examples. If this is new to you, back up one level on that page to
gain access to the full set of on-line help pages for ggplot2:
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/  As you scroll toward the bottom of the
page, you'll find them. It's worth bookmarking.

The change I mentioned is found in scale_x_date(). The package is
undergoing a renovation of sorts, and one of the changes is to make
the syntax of functions starting with scale_ more consistent. In the
new version, you can tailor certain types of axis labeling with
functions that end in _format; these are found in the scales package.
Since you're new to ggplot2, it's probably better to wait a few days
until the new version is released so that you don't have to 'unlearn'
the old way of doing things. One of the advantages of the new version
is that the help pages have many more examples, so it should be a bit
easier to pick up how things work from the help pages as well as the
on-line help. And of course there is this group if you get hopelessly
stuck.

One thing I've avoided mentioning here but which is important to know
when learning ggplot2 is the distinction between mapping and setting
aesthetics. An aesthetic is mapped if it is associated with a
variable, and is set if it is a fixed value. Mapped aesthetics are
defined inside an aes() statement within a ggplot() or a geom_() call;
those that are set are specified outside an aes() statement. In this
example, the only time aes() was invoked was within ggplot() - every
other aesthetic (e.g., color, size, yintercept) was set. It's worth
taking the time to understand this distinction - it will save you a
lot of frustration later.

HTH,
Dennis

Hi:

Run str(xp). If date is not a Date object, then scale_x_date() will
throw an error. If it is a POSIXct object, try using
scale_x_datetime() instead; check out its help page at
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/scale_datetime.html to find its arguments
(for 0.8.9 - they will change in 0.9.0). There is no example on that
page using POSIXct objects, but scale_x_datetime() can work with them.
I found a few examples by searching the archives of this group with
the string 'POSIXct datetime' and browsing the list of posts that was
returned.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: ggplot2 output not showing in script
messages.subject_clean: ggplot2 output not showing in script
messages.body_plain:
I was practicing R and ggplot so I made a fake data set and did some
calculations and graphs in a script.  I have a combination of R's base
graphics and also ggplot's graphics.  When I run the script--
source('myfile.R')--it skips over the boxplot, q-q plot, and all of
the ggplots.  The graphs that do display are the histogram and the
plot(lmfit)  What is happening here?

#create emr records data
emr=cbind(rep(factor('emr'),
50),rnorm(50,mean=250,sd=30),rnorm(50,mean=3,sd=1))
emr=data.frame(emr)
emr[,1]=factor('emr')
colnames(emr)=c('records','cost','numlabs')
#create paper records data
paper=cbind(rep(factor('paper'),
50),rnorm(50,mean=325,sd=30),rnorm(50,mean=6,sd=1))
paper=data.frame(paper)
paper[,1]=factor('paper')
colnames(paper)=colnames(emr)
#create mixed data
mixed=cbind(rep(factor('mixed'),
50),rnorm(50,mean=290,sd=15),rnorm(50,mean=4.6,sd=.5))
mixed=data.frame(mixed)
mixed[,1]=factor('mixed')
colnames(mixed)=colnames(emr)
#combine the three into one data frame and round the labs to integers
recordsdata=rbind(emr,paper)
recordsdata=rbind(recordsdata,mixed)
recordsdata$numlabs=round(recordsdata$numlabs)
print(recordsdata)
#linear model of records data
lmfit=lm(formula=recordsdata$cost~recordsdata$records)
#some useful plots
boxplot(recordsdata$cost~recordsdata$records)
qqnorm(emr$cost)
hist(emr$cost)
#pretty density plot
library(ggplot2)
qplot(recordsdata$cost)
ggplot(recordsdata,aes(cost,fill=records))
+geom_density(alpha=0.2)+xlim(140,400)
ggplot(recordsdata,aes(cost,fill=records))+geom_histogram()
plot(lmfit)

OK, there is an issue with time zone conversion with this method.

Where I live is CST (GMT -6). Posix 0 is not 0:00:00 1-1-1970, it's 18:00:00 12-31-1969. So I can't range from 0 to 86399; I have to range from 0+ 21600 to 86399+21600, which is 21600 to 107999. (21600 is the number of seconds in 6 hours.)

How do I tell ggplot2 to not attempt to convert for time zones?

Aren

messages.body_plain:
I realized this text is very dense and hard to read so I separated
things out better.  Here's a link to the script I made:
http://dl.dropbox.com/u/1852742/fakeemrdata.R
Thanks to Dennis Murphy for some tips on cleaning up the data creation
in the beginning.  The changes are reflected here.

And here it is pasted:

#I created some fake EMR data with a function that generates random
data that
#is in roughly a normal distribution.  I can set the approx. mean and
sd
#as well.  The final data frame is called "recordsdata".  I ran tests
and made
#plots and tables that will be useful.  Note that if you were typing
these
#commands in R itself you don't have to use the print command.

#create emr records data
emr=data.frame(records=factor(rep('emr',50)),
cost=rnorm(50,mean=250,sd=30),
numlabs=rnorm(50,mean=3,sd=1))

#create paper records data
paper=data.frame(records=factor(rep('paper',50)),
cost=rnorm(50,mean=325,sd=30),
numlabs=rnorm(50,mean=6,sd=1))

#create mixed data
mixed=data.frame(records=factor(rep('mixed',50)),
cost=rnorm(50,mean=290,sd=15),
numlabs=rnorm(50,mean=4.6,sd=.5))

#combine the three into one data frame and round the labs to integers
recordsdata=rbind(emr,paper)
recordsdata=rbind(recordsdata,mixed)
recordsdata$numlabs=round(recordsdata$numlabs)
print(recordsdata)

#write the data frame to csv
#write.csv(recordsdata,file='foobar.csv')

#show summary by type of records
print(tapply(recordsdata$cost,recordsdata$records,summary))
print(tapply(recordsdata$cost,recordsdata$records,sd))

#two-way table of records means
recordstable=table(recordsdata$records,recordsdata
$cost>mean(recordsdata$cost))
print(recordstable)

#summary of table including chi-square
print(summary(recordstable))

#linear model of records data
lmfit=lm(formula=recordsdata$cost~recordsdata$records)

print(summary(lmfit))

#anova of lmfit
print(anova(lmfit))

#pair-wise t test of records data
print(pairwise.t.test(recordsdata$cost,recordsdata
$records,pool.sd <http://pool.sd>=FALSE))

#some useful plots
boxplot(recordsdata$cost~recordsdata$records,ylab='Cost (Dollars)')
qqnorm(emr$cost)
hist(emr$cost)

#pretty ggplot plots
library(ggplot2)
qplot(recordsdata$cost)

#another
ggplot(recordsdata,aes(cost,fill=records))+geom_density(alpha=0.2)+
scale_x_continuous('Cost (Dollars)',limits=c(150,425))

#another
ggplot(recordsdata,aes(cost,fill=records))+geom_histogram()

#plots for the linear model
plot(lmfit)

messages.body_plain:
If you want the old labeling, a 'simple' way to do it in 0.9.0 is to
transform carat and then use math_format() to get the labeling to look
like 0.8.9:

library('ggplot2')    # 0.9.0 development version
library('scales')

qplot(log10(carat), price, data = diamonds) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = 'carat', labels = math_format(10^.x))

The advantage of using log10(carat) in the qplot call is that the
default breaks from qplot() are the exponents you want to pass to
math_format().

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: How to stop ggplot2 from converting POSIX from GMT to CST?
messages.subject_clean: How to stop ggplot2 from converting POSIX from GMT to CST?
messages.body_plain:
Sorry if I wandered too much with my prior emails. Let me rephrase.

Short version:
ggplot is converting my POSIX time values from GMT to CST (GMT-6), which is my time zone. How do I stop this?

Long version:
I have a data frame. It has a column with POSIX time values like this:
3840 6780 36480 7200 46740 13500 64800 44400 46800 42000 14400 39660 5100 36600 33600 79620
(spaces separate different values).

All the values are between 0 and 86399, representing times between 0:00 (midnight) and 23:59:59. Technically the date is 1-1-1970, but I am ignoring the date.

The problem is if I plot them in a histogram. Suppose I use this:
p <- qplot(dallas$offense_posix) + xlab("Offense time") + scale_x_datetime(format = "%H:00")
print(p)

The X axis values start with 18:00 12-31-1969 and end with 17:59 1-1-1970. It's as if ggplot2 is assuming the POSIX times are in GMT and converting them to CST.

How do I tell ggplot2 to ignore time zones? I've looked through the ggplot book and checked other online resources and cannot find a clear answer. I'm sure it's something novice I'm missing, so sorry if this is a stupid question.

Aren

I found the tz parameter on scale_x_datetime.

If I don't specify a tz value, the values run from 18:00 12-31-1969 to 17:59 1-1-1970.
If I use tz="GMT", the values go 06:00:00 1/1/1970 to 05:59:59 01/02/1970.
If I use tz="CST", I get In as.POSIXlt.POSIXct(x, tz) : unknown timezone 'CST'
If I use tz="", I get correct values!

Aren

messages.subject: Re: chapter 5, pp. 67-68
messages.subject_clean: chapter 5, pp. 67-68
messages.body_plain:
I mentioned this a few weeks ago on the ggplot2-dev list. The problem
is that you have label as an aesthetic in the original ggplot() call
and ggplot2 expects to see it in every subsequent layer. One
workaround is to add group = 1 as an aesthetic:

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y, label = label, group = 1)) + xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL)

Now rerun the plot calls again and they should work. I just checked
several of them in the upcoming version 0.9.0 and they all worked fine
with the above change. It should be the same in 0.8.9. [Aside: There
will be a few other places where the book code breaks when the new
version is released, so be prepared.]

Taking label out of the aes() statement in ggplot() would also work:

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL)

The only line of code you would need to change would be the one
involving the label in geom_text():

p + geom_text(aes(label = label)) + opts(title = "geom_text")

This would be the preferred way of doing things because the variables
mapped in ggplot() through aes() are expected to be present in every
subsequent layer of the plot. You can always add aesthetics in a
geom_*() call, and in fact it's  done rather often, even in the book.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2 forum!

I would like to plot barplots (continuos variable on y axis,
categorical on x axis) while facetting over another categorical
variable. I am using scale="free_x" to drop missing factor levels.
However (see dummy example below) this leads to equal width of the
facet plots but unequal width of the plotted bars. I would like the
opposite: equal width of the bars and unequal width of the single
facet plots. I think otherwise different bar width is misleading.

Thanks for your help!

data <- diamonds[1:10,]
data$cut <- as.factor(as.character(data$cut))
data$color <- as.factor(as.character(data$color))
d <- ggplot(data, aes(cut,carat))
d + geom_bar(stat="identity")+ facet_grid(.~ color,scale="free_x")

I am trying to change the legend.text for a continuous scale
variable.

I have a large amount of data (~60000 records) and I want a scatter
graph to show the distribution (code below).  I have used the
stat_binhex to capture this.  Due to the counts varying from very
small numbers (one record per cell) up to very large counts (5000+), I
have used a log transformation in the scale_fill_continuous function.
The graph looks exactly how I want.

The legend however, report powers of 10^0, 10^0.5 etc.  I would like
to over write this with my own text (eg "Very few", "Few" etc).  How
do I do this? (I have spent nearly an entire day trying to find a
solution - admittedly I only started using ggplot2 on Monday and I
have produced a graph that is way better than I hoped for but I would
like to make it that little bit better :))

thanks

Jaron

d_fp_nho <- ggplot(my_data, aes(my_x,my_y)) +
scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 300)) + scale_x_continuous(limits =
c(0, 160))  + xlab("Before") + ylab("After")  + opts(title = "FP
NHO")

FP_NHO_data <- d_fp_nho + stat_binhex(binwidth=c(2,2)) +
coord_equal(ratio = 1) + scale_fill_continuous(low="grey", high="red",
limits=c(1,5000),trans="log10")

messages.subject_clean: Equal bar width while using facet_grid
messages.body_plain:
On 1/10/2012 10:50 PM, Jokel Meyer wrote:
> Thank you very much for the quick answer!
>
> I was wondering why this works fine until you used coord_flip()?

coord_flip() is evil.  Wait, that is too harsh.  coord_flip() is more
likely to cause problems than it is to solve them.  I have a personal
(although practical) vendetta against it.

This is a good example; there is no way to do what you want to do.
space="free" does nothing in the presence of coord_flip().  The
"correct" solution is a geom which draws horizontal bars.  See
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/msg/24400aadbbb9bc8e for some
code which can do that.  Actually that entire thread
(http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/583fcfdced24b483/)
addresses this problem.

> data<- diamonds[1:10,]
> data$cut<- as.factor(as.character(data$cut))
> data$color<- as.factor(as.character(data$color))
> d<- ggplot(data, aes(cut,carat))
> d + geom_bar(stat="identity")+ facet_grid(color~.,scale="free_x",
> space="free")
>
> How could you plot the above example with even bar widths and skipping
> unused factor levels?
> Many thanks!

With the above mentioned custom geom, you could then have

ggplot(data, aes(carat, cut)) +
   geom_hbar() +
   facet_grid(color ~ ., scale="free_y", space="free")

Figure 1 has in  2 tables  below the plot.

So with the colon data and using he excellent function ggkm from
Abhijit http://statbandit.wordpress.com/2011/03/08/an-enhanced-kaplan-meier-plot/

which work beautifully for one table,

 I have generated to code below and manage to get my 2 tables
data.tablerisk and data.tableevent.

I have no clue on how to play with
plot.margin = unit(c(0, 1, .5, ifelse(m < 10, 1.5, 2.5)), "lines")

and

grid.arrange(p, blank.pic, data.tablerisk, #data.tableevent,
        clip = FALSE, nrow = 3, ncol = 1,
        heights = unit(c(1.5, .1, .25),c("null", "null", "null")))

so that I can get the 2 tables below the plot. I have not found
documentation to assist me understanding how that works.

The other problem I have is to produce the "At risk" and "Death/
censored" headings in bold which in the function is produced below the
table by
 scale_x_continuous("Numbers at risk", limits = c(0, max(sfit$time)))

and I need to have it above the table.

Any help will be very much appreciated.

Best wishes, JL

library(ggplot2)
library(plyr)
library(scales)
library(gridExtra)
library(ggExtra)
library(survival)
#data
data(colon)
sfit <- survfit(Surv(time,status)~rx, data=colon)
#################
#parameters
table = TRUE
returns = FALSE
xlabs = "Time Since Randomization (Days)"
ylabs = "Cumulative Survival"
ystratalabs = NULL
ystrataname = NULL
timeby = 500
main = NULL
pval = TRUE
#############END initial
if(is.null(ystratalabs)) {
   ystratalabs <- as.character(levels(summary(sfit)$strata))
}
ystratalabs <- sub("treatment=","",ystratalabs)#cas particulier
m <- max(nchar(ystratalabs))
if(is.null(ystrataname)) ystrataname <- ""
times <- seq(0, max(sfit$time), by = timeby)
.df <- data.frame(time = sfit$time, n.risk = sfit$n.risk,
    n.event = sfit$n.event, surv = sfit$surv, strata = summary(sfit,
censored = T)$strata,
    upper = sfit$upper, lower = sfit$lower)
levels(.df$strata) <- ystratalabs
zeros <- data.frame(time = 0, surv = 1, strata = factor(ystratalabs,
levels=levels(.df$strata)),
    upper = 1, lower = 1)
.df <- rbind.fill(zeros, .df)
d <- length(levels(.df$strata))
#
p <- ggplot(.df, aes(time, surv, groups = strata)) +
    geom_step(aes(linetype = strata, colour = strata), size = 0.7) +
#	geom_point(aes(colour = strata), shape = 3 , size=1.5) +
	 theme_bw() +
    opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(vjust = 0.5)) +
    scale_x_continuous(xlabs, breaks = times, limits = c(0, max(sfit
$time))) +
    scale_y_continuous(ylabs, limits = c(0, 1), breaks=seq(0,1,0.1)) +
	 scale_colour_discrete(name=ystrataname) +
	 scale_linetype_discrete(name=ystrataname) +
     opts(panel.grid.minor = theme_blank()) +
    opts(legend.position = c(ifelse(m < 10, .25, .35), ifelse(d < 4, .
50, .65))) +
    opts(legend.key = theme_rect(colour = NA)) +
 #   labs(linetype = ystrataname) +
    opts(plot.margin = unit(c(0, 1, .5, ifelse(m < 10, 1.5, 2.5)),
"lines")) +
    opts(title = main)

## Create a blank plot for place-holding
blank.pic <- ggplot(.df, aes(time, surv)) +
    geom_blank() +
    theme_bw() +
    opts(axis.text.x = theme_blank(), axis.text.y = theme_blank(),
        axis.title.x = theme_blank(), axis.title.y = theme_blank(),
        axis.ticks = theme_blank(), panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
        panel.border = theme_blank())
if(pval) {
    sdiff <- survdiff(eval(sfit$call$formula), data = eval(sfit$call
$data))
    pval <- pchisq(sdiff$chisq, length(sdiff$n) - 1, lower.tail =
FALSE)
    pvaltxt <- ifelse(pval < 0.0001, "p < 0.0001", paste("p =",
signif(pval, 3)))
    p <- p + annotate("text", x = 0.6 * max(sfit$time), y = 0.1, label
= pvaltxt)
}
if(table) {
    ## Create table graphic to include at-risk numbers
    risk.data <- data.frame(strata = summary(sfit, times = times,
extend = TRUE)$strata,
        time = summary(sfit, times = times, extend = TRUE)$time,
        n.risk = summary(sfit, times = times, extend = TRUE)$n.risk)
	## Create table to include events
	event.data <- data.frame(strata = summary(sfit, times = times, extend
= TRUE)$strata,
        time = summary(sfit, times = times, extend = TRUE)$time,
       n.event = summary(sfit, times = times, extend = TRUE)$n.event)
	event <- ddply(event.data, .(strata), transform,
                     cevent = cumsum(n.event))
#
    data.tablerisk <- ggplot(risk.data, aes(x = time, y = strata,
	   label = format(n.risk, nsmall = 0))) +
        #, color = strata)) +
        geom_text(size = 3.5) +
        theme_bw() +
        scale_y_discrete(breaks = as.character(levels(risk.data
$strata)), labels = ystratalabs) +
        scale_x_continuous("Numbers at risk", limits = c(0, max(sfit
$time))) +
        opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 10, vjust = 1),
panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(), panel.border =
theme_blank(),
        axis.text.x = theme_blank(), axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
        axis.text.y = theme_text(face = "bold", hjust = 1))
    data.tablerisk <- data.tablerisk + opts(legend.position = "none")
+
        xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL)
    data.tablerisk <- data.tablerisk +
        opts(plot.margin = unit(c(-1.5, 1, 0.1, ifelse(m < 10, 2.5,
3.5) - 0.28 * m), "lines"))
#
 data.tableevent <- ggplot(event, aes(x = time, y = strata,
	   label = format(cevent, nsmall = 0))) +
        #, color = strata)) +
        geom_text(size = 3.5) +
        theme_bw() +
        scale_y_discrete(breaks = as.character(levels(risk.data

$time))) +
        opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 10, vjust = 1),
panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(), panel.border =
theme_blank(),
        axis.text.x = theme_blank(), axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
        axis.text.y = theme_text(face = "bold", hjust = 1))
    data.tableevent <- data.tableevent + opts(legend.position =

        xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL)
    data.tableevent <- data.tableevent +

0.28 * m), "lines"))

## Plotting the graphs
        grid.arrange(p, blank.pic, data.tablerisk, #data.tableevent,

    }

messages.subject_clean: Sharing a legend between multiple plots in 0.9
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The LearnR example can be replicated using Baptiste's suggestion
(thank you very much!!) as follows in 0.9.0 - it isn't just plug and
play, the legend has to be positioned in the right place. This should
be recorded in the archives until a better way comes along.

library('ggplot2')   # 0.9.0
library('grid')
p <- qplot(data = mtcars, mpg, hp, geom = "point",
     colour = cyl)
p1 <- p + opts(legend.position = "none")
p2 <- qplot(data = mtcars, wt, disp, geom = "point",
     colour = cyl) + opts(legend.position = "none")

Layout <- grid.layout(nrow = 2, ncol = 2,
                      widths = unit(c(2, 0.4), c("null", "null")),
                      heights = unit(c(1, 1), c("null", "null")))
vplayout <- function(...) {
     grid.newpage()
     pushViewport(viewport(layout = Layout))
 }
subplot <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row = x,
     layout.pos.col = y)

g <- ggplotGrob(p)

# Notice that the viewport location is defined here:
legend <- editGrob( getGrob( g, gPath("guide"), grep=TRUE, global=TRUE ),
                   vp= subplot(1:2, 2) )

vplayout()
print(p1, vp = subplot(1, 1))
print(p2, vp = subplot(2, 1))
grid.draw(legend)

Dennis

X

# Works but is a bit clunky
Y<-subset(X,complete.cases(X))

# I like using matrix indexing and I think this is the simplest way to
do this...

move the comma.
Y<-X[ , complete.cases(X)]

messages.body_plain:
This is only partly ggplot2, but I think many members will the same question.

I'm trying to make some basic maps in ggplot2 and having trouble with the syntax for importing shapes for a map of Japan. Using geom_point is simple since I have the latitude, longitude and magnitude data , but how do I get the underlying map to use with geom_line? I assume the syntax should be something like this for a file on the gadm server

> borders.mp <http://borders.mp> <- readShapePoly("http://gadm.org/data/rda/JPN_adm2.RData")

but that generates

Error in the.map$names : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors

What is the structure of an .RData file?

Thanks,
Mark

messages.subject: Re: OHLC/candlestick stock prices
messages.subject_clean: OHLC/candlestick stock prices
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Kohske,

geom_segment worked better than a - glyph for geom_point.

also fixed the grouping in the boxplot so the candles look OK.

here is where it ended up. would like to have the holidays not show up
as missing candles, fix the legend/color mapping, but should be a
starting point for anyone who wants to do OHLC and candlesticks.
Pretty popular in finance, was surprised not to be able to Google for
a ggplot example.

require(quantmod)
require(ggplot2)

############################################################
# ggplot OHLC tick chart
############################################################

getSymbols(c('^GSPC'), src="yahoo")
GSPC = na.omit(GSPC)

GSPC<-GSPC['2011-09-01::']

dfSP =data.frame(GSPC)
dfSP$date=as.Date(rownames(dfSP))

# open/high/low/close
ggplot(data=dfSP, aes(x=date)) +
 opts(title="S&P Index") +
 ylab("S&P Index") +
 theme_bw() +
 geom_linerange(aes(ymin=GSPC.Low, ymax=GSPC.High)) +
 geom_segment(aes(y = GSPC.Open, yend = GSPC.Open, xend = date - 0.5))
+
 geom_segment(aes(y = GSPC.Close, yend = GSPC.Close, xend = date +
0.5))

############################################################
# ggplot Candlestick chart
############################################################

getSymbols(c('^GSPC'), src="yahoo")
GSPC = na.omit(GSPC)
GSPClag = lag(GSPC,1)
GSPC<-GSPC['2011-09-01::']
GSPClag<-GSPClag['2011-09-01::']

dfSP =data.frame(GSPC)
dfSP$date=as.Date(rownames(dfSP))

lagdfSP=data.frame(GSPClag)
lagdfSP$date=as.Date(rownames(lagdfSP))
keep=c('date', 'GSPC.Close')
lagdfSP=lagdfSP[keep]
names(lagdfSP) = c( "date","GSPC.Prev")
dfSP <- merge(dfSP, lagdfSP, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)

dfSP$candle_lower = pmin(dfSP$GSPC.Open, dfSP$GSPC.Close)
dfSP$candle_upper = pmax(dfSP$GSPC.Open, dfSP$GSPC.Close)
dfSP$candle_middle = NA

dfSP$up = dfSP$GSPC.Close> dfSP$GSPC.Prev
dfSP$fill = ''
dfSP$fill[dfSP$GSPC.Close > dfSP$GSPC.Open] = 'white'
dfSP$fill[(dfSP$fill =='') & (dfSP$up==TRUE)] = 'green'
dfSP$fill[dfSP$fill ==''] = 'red'

green = "#4daf4a"
red = "#e41a1c"

ggplot(data=dfSP,aes(x=date, y=GSPC.Close, ymin=GSPC.Low,
ymax=GSPC.High,
lower=candle_lower, middle=candle_middle, upper=candle_upper)) +
opts(title="S&P Index") +
ylab("S&P Index") +
theme_bw() +
geom_boxplot(stat='identity', aes(fill=fill, color=factor(up),
group=date))+
scale_colour_manual(values = c(red,green)) +
scale_fill_manual(values = c(red, green,'white'))

messages.subject: Re: Importing map files for ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: Importing map files for ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
fortify.SpatialPolygonsDataFrame exists for exactly this purpose:

library(ggplot2)
library(plyr)
library(maptools)

load(url("http://gadm.org/data/rda/JPN_adm2.RData"))

# restricted licence (see:
http://www.cs.man.ac.uk/~toby/alan/software/#Licensing)
gpclibPermit()

# which variable identifies polygons?
head(as.data.frame(gadm))
# looks like ID_2

# convert to a structure ggplot2 can handle...takes a while
japan_map <- fortify(gadm, region = "ID_2")

# join up the useful names
japan_map <- rename(japan_map, c("id" = "ID_2"))
japan_map <- join(japan_map,
  as.data.frame(gadm)[, c("ID_2", "NAME_1", "NAME_2")])

# a subset for speed
qplot(long, lat, data = subset(japan_map, NAME_1 == "Miyagi"),
  geom = "path", group = group)

# filled polygons
qplot(long, lat, data = subset(japan_map, NAME_1 == "Miyagi"),
  geom = "polygon", group = group)

# everything = SLOW!
qplot(long, lat, data = japan_map, geom = "path", group = group)

# everything, filled polygons
qplot(long, lat, data = japan_map, geom = "polygon", group = group)

Hope that helps,

Charlotte

> scale_x_continuous(), a half dozen others. The closest I got was this:

>> trans_breaks('log10', function(x) 10^x)(diamonds$carat)
> [1] 0.1584893 0.2511886 0.3981072 0.6309573 1.0000000 1.5848932 2.5118864
> [8] 3.9810717 6.3095734
> log10(trans_breaks('log10', function(x) 10^x)(diamonds$carat))
> [1] -0.8 -0.6 -0.4 -0.2  0.0  0.2  0.4  0.6  0.8
>
> This gives the right values for the exponents, but it's a pretty
> convoluted way of getting them. The problem is that if you use this in
> conjunction with scale_x_continuous's labels = argument using
> math_format(), the position of the tick marks is all wrong. Try this:

>
> This is basically a reflection of your tick mark positions around 1.
> If there's a way to get a linear scale with math_format() using
> scale_x_continuous() and its breaks = and values = arguments, I
> haven't found it yet.
>
> I *think* the problem is that qplot() is plotting in the original
> metric for carat, so there's no way it can render a linear scale in
> the exponents. Here's one example I tried with coord_trans():
>

>
> last_plot() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 10^lb, labels =
> math_format(10^.x)(lb))

Isn't what you want:

qplot(carat, price, data = diamonds) +

    scale_x_log10(labels = math_format())

What am I missing?

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
I know I'm moving past the initial scope of ggplot2 with this, but if
anyone have some ideas for how to accomplish this (with hacks if
necessary) I would be grateful.

Im using ggplot2 and ggdendro to create transcriptomic-like heatmaps
for peptide-intensity data (http://dl.dropbox.com/u/2323585/
AA1251heat.png). What I would like to do (and have crudely attempted
in the supplied graph) is to create an additional panel between the
heatmap and the dendrogram, holding colour coded information about
some covariate. In a perfect world this should also be done
vertically.

The most natural way would be to use geom_tile() in order to ensure
allignment, but as the scale_fill() is already used in the heatmap-
panel I cannot use this scale for another variable with a new colour
scheme.

Is there any way to add additional scales of the same type, however
cumbersome it is (e.g. manually create a scale_fill2 function and
setting fill2 instead of fill in the geom_tile)...

The code used can be found here: http://dl.dropbox.com/u/2323585/ggHeat.R

Note it uses some hacks proprietary of baptiste to alter the aspect
ratios of the facets: http://dl.dropbox.com/u/2323585/ggplot%20grid%20mod.r

Thanks for the help in advance...

Thomas Pedersen

messages.subject: Re: Change lineend for geom_segment()
messages.subject_clean: Change lineend for geom_segment()
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

There's support for this in the upcoming (currently development)
version of ggplot2 (0.9.0), where geom_path() has a new argument
lineend:

lineend   Line end style (round, butt, square)

You could wait for the new version (should be soon but no official ETA
yet), or you could install the development version of 0.9.0 as
follows:

library('devtools')   # install from CRAN first if necessary
dev_mode()
install_github('ggplot2')    # current development version
library('ggplot2')
<your code>

Caution: there are a number of new functions and features, some of
which may break old code. Alternatively, the new code may help you
figure out how to modify the function(s) of interest in 0.8.9.

Dennis

messages.subject_clean: Histogram with different color fillings
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working on a histogram where certain regions (based on quantiles)
have different colors. I found on this discussion list an answer how
to do this with two different regions, using a logical statement for
fill. How could I this with multiple?

An example
df <- data.frame(x=rnorm(10000))
g <- ggplot(data=df,  aes(x=x))
g <- g + geom_histogram()
print(g)

I would like to fill the histogram with different colors for these
regions (for example) (-Inf, -2], (-2,2], and (2, Inf).

Thanks so much.
T

messages.subject: Suggestion: documentation improvements
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: documentation improvements
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A bit of background: I have taught R and ggplot in particular for 3
years now and follow closely the development of ggplot. After this
year's classes, I collected a few suggestions that Hadley asked me to
bring to the list for discussion. If you have remarks or can also
provide feedback regarding how newcomers fare with ggplot, they would
enrich the discussion.

My point of view is: ggplot2 is still in version < 1.0, if things
don't get broken for the sake of improvement now, they never will …
except in a hypothetical ggplot3 but that wouldn't be a good idea.
This is why some of the changes I suggest might be a bit radical. In
all cases I think they would be worth it (even though I have a *lot*
of ggplot code that would need to be updated). It would be good to
know what other people think.

Improving the documentation would greatly ease the discovery of
ggplot. I used the stable version because I did not want to get into
trouble with the dev one with students. I know lots of improvements
are coming which is great. It might need to go a little further:
	. detail of the statistics computed by geoms, when they do;
	. advice on usage such as with geom_point;
	. more links between functions in the See Also part;
	. but, at the same time, better compartmentalization within the help
of each function (i.e. do not use stuff that are potentially not yet
known by the user).

In particular, an homogenous syntax in the example section would be
much welcome, at least for the first few examples of each geom. I
understand Hadley probably wanted to mix qplot, ggplot, p <- ggplot()
+ … and all the other niceties and richness of ggplot. But that makes
it harder to teach and understand. In geom_point (probably the first
everyone looks at) the data and aes are specified first in ggplot and
then in the geom call, the aesthetic call does not explicitly specify
the arguments etc. I would suggest:
	. use :
		ggplot() + geom_***(mapping=aes(x=foo, y=bar), data=myD)
	as the default notation, in full, everywhere. It is the most
versatile (save for layer(), but that is almost never used) and the
most consistent.
	. then in later examples, introduce the refinements/shortcuts such as:
		- omitting argument names
		- specifying stuff within the ggplot() call, that will be inherited
		- storing the plot as an object and modifying it afterwards
		- using qplot

Finally, separating "drawing geoms" (those for which stat="identify")
and "statistical geoms" (those in which computation is made on the
data before plotting) on the website and in the doc would help
regarding teaching (e.g. "Start with the basics, then dive into more
complex stuff").

JiHO
---

messages.subject: Suggestion: use stat_identity as default for geom_bar
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: use stat_identity as default for geom_bar
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

geom_bar with its non-"identity" statistic confuses novice users and
forces them to learn about the stat argument (and statistics in
general in the grammar of graphics) which greatly complicates a first
approach to ggplot.

I suggested this in the past (and I know it would break existing code)
but I think geom_bar should default to stat="identity". At least, this
should be the case when y is supplied, which would limit the backward
compatibility problem. The requirement for stat="bin" is reduced by
the existence of geom_histogram anyway.

What does a "barplot" mean to most people? To me it just means a graph
with vertical bars, not necessarily a histogram, hence my expectation
that y should be specified and give the height of the bars.

JiHO
---

messages.subject: Suggestion: simplification of scales by using higher level functions
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: simplification of scales by using higher level functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

scales are quite hard to get through to students and newcomers to
ggplot. In particular, it seems silly to them that they have to write

	scale_x_continuous(name="My x scale")

just to change the title of the axis. I know about xlab() or
update_labels() but I want to use and teach the proper and most
versatile way of doing things, before getting to the shorthands. I
think that's the best for students in the end. Why wouldn't

	scale_x()

suffice? It is not possible to get two x (or y) scales (and, from what
I can see from Hadley's comments on this mailing list, there never
will, which is good) so the user shouldn't have to care wether the
scale is continuous or discrete or a date or … ggplot should deduce it
from the data and act accordingly.
Colour/fill is potentially more complex because there could indeed be
two colour scales on the same plot:

	d <- data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10), z=runif(10),
w=factor(round(runif(10)*3)))
	ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point(aes(colour=w)) + geom_path(aes(colour=z))

But that currently is not allowed. I reported it as a bug but it was
actually considered a feature IIRC. In that case, it would be much
easier to just have scale_colour() and scale_fill() and, again, decide
on the behaviour based on the nature of the data.

The homogeneity between the arguments of all the scales (name, breaks,
labels, etc.) would justify and ease the use of these "higher level"
functions. Of course some arguments are specific and the continuous
and discrete cases should be distinguished in the help but having
these simpler more "intelligent" functions as the main front end would
be way better I think.

messages.subject: Suggestion: reorganisation and renaming of colour scales
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: reorganisation and renaming of colour scales
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

The gradients scales could be greatly simplified: gradient, gradient2,
gradientn... all this is complex.
Basically, scale_gradient should be the only interface, behave like
scale_gradientn and have a midpoint argument, NULL by default, which,
when specified, makes it behave like scale_gradient2. I thought I read
it was improved in the new version although I cannot see it in the dev
version I have at the moment.

scale_colour_hue is difficult to understand by novice,
non-graphic-oriented users (particularly non-english speaking ones).
What about scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous, to match
with all the rest of the scales?

Finally, the fact that "colour" affects the inside of objects for
geom_point but the outside for most others is bad for consistency and
hence learning and discovery. What about having separate fill and
stroke for all geoms (with stroke basically replacing colour
currently)? And then have colour do something "intelligent" depending
on the scale (i.e. stroke for path, fill for polygon, fill for tile
etc.). That would give fine, consistent control when needed
(fill/stroke) but also allow a more natural approach ("I want this to
be *coloured* according to that", without having to care what the
colour is applied to). This simpler approach would probably suffice
for the majority of users (very rarely do I use both fill and stroke
colours on the same object).

I understand this would also cause a backward compatibility problem
(using both fill and colour on something where colour would refere to
fill) but again, that would be the price for a better behaviour in the
end.

JiHO
---

messages.subject: Suggestion: complete make over for the theming mechanism
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: complete make over for the theming mechanism
messages.body_plain:
Hi all... one last time!

theming is *really* cumbersome at the moment. I would go as far as
saying it is currently the weakest aspect of ggplot2. Switching themes
completely (as is often required by journals) is not so hard with
theme_bw available. But just changing something like the orientation
of the text on a scale, which is often required (e.g. long names for
categories in x), requires to use opts and theme_text and to know the
defaults for the parameters other than orientation etc.
update_element() seems to help but it is difficult to discover.

I really think that the whole theming approach based on functions is
problematic. In my opinion, it would only add functionality if one
could use different functions for each theme element… but I don't see
how you would use theme_rect for an axis legend or theme_text for the
background of the plot. So I suggest to scratch this and replace it
with a simple hierachical named list such that theme_gray would
become:

	axis.line = NA
	axis.text.x = list
		axis.text.x$family = "Helvetica"
		axis.text.x$size = 10
		axis.text.x$lineheight = 0.9
		axis.text.x$colour = "grey50"
		etc.
	axis.text.y = list
		axis.text.x$family = "Helvetica"
		etc.

That way you could modify independently each element of the theme
without having to know about new functions, just by navigating a list
e.g. opts(axis.text.x$orientation=45).
This also means that users would have access to each element of the
current theme and do things like "annotate the plot with a vertical
line *the same colour as the current grid*". And this would work even
when the whole theme is changed and the grid becomes black for
example, which is currently impossible.

Combined with adding constants to the list such as the existing:
	. base_size
	. base_family
but also
	. base_fill
	. base_stroke
this would also allow to change the default colour used by ggplot own
geoms (currently black for points/lines and something like "grey20"
for fills) and make it easier to affect the whole plot.

For example, if I want all plots to have a blue-ish aspect to fit with
the design of a given piece of work, I can change the grid background
with the theme but I have to set colour/fill="myBlue" for every plot.
Cumbersome. I suspect this "complete" theming approach would prove
popular with design-nerds and this is an audience ggplot2 has interest
in pleasing (they are the ones that make ggplot look good on the web)
and almost has the means to please.

JiHO
---

messages.subject: Re: Suggestion: use stat_identity as default for geom_bar
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: use stat_identity as default for geom_bar
messages.body_plain:
This sounds like a good suggestion to me. I recall being a bit confused in the beginning about when geom_bar would display counts, and when it would display the y values.

Here are some examples:

# Display counts. (stat="bin" is the default)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl))) + geom_bar(stat="bin")

# Error, because using stat="identity" without specifying y
# (It is good that it throws an error)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl))) + geom_bar(stat="identity")

# If we add y mapping, it will stack y values, which can also be confusing
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl), y=mpg)) + geom_bar(stat="identity")

# Error, because using stat="bin" with multiple y values.
# This behavior can be confusing.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl), y=mpg)) + geom_bar(stat="bin")

# This works and gives the same output for "bin" and "identity":
# Pull out one instance each of cyl==4, 6, and 8
ggplot(mtcars[c(1,3,5),], aes(x=factor(cyl), y=mpg)) + geom_bar(stat="bin")
ggplot(mtcars[c(1,3,5),], aes(x=factor(cyl), y=mpg)) + geom_bar(stat="identity")

One the whole, I'd say that using stat="identity" as the default is slightly less confusing than stat="bin". But even with this change, it can still be a bit confusing when there are multiple y values at a single x, because the bars get stacked, and by default it looks like a single bar because they don't have visible outlines.

I don't think that the default stat should be conditional on whether a y mapping is provided -- I think the small benefit would be outweighed by the added complexity and inconsistent behavior.

-Winston

On Wed, Jan 18, 2012 at 4:10 PM, JiHO <jo.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> geom_bar with its non-"identity" statistic confuses novice users and
> forces them to learn about the stat argument (and statistics in
> general in the grammar of graphics) which greatly complicates a first
> approach to ggplot.
>
> I suggested this in the past (and I know it would break existing code)
> but I think geom_bar should default to stat="identity". At least, this
> should be the case when y is supplied, which would limit the backward
> compatibility problem. The requirement for stat="bin" is reduced by
> the existence of geom_histogram anyway.
>
> What does a "barplot" mean to most people? To me it just means a graph
> with vertical bars, not necessarily a histogram, hence my expectation
> that y should be specified and give the height of the bars.
>
> JiHO

messages.subject: Re: Suggestion: reorganisation and renaming of colour scales
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: reorganisation and renaming of colour scales
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Jan 18, 2012 at 4:11 PM, JiHO <jo.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> The gradients scales could be greatly simplified: gradient, gradient2,
> gradientn... all this is complex.
> Basically, scale_gradient should be the only interface, behave like
> scale_gradientn and have a midpoint argument, NULL by default, which,
> when specified, makes it behave like scale_gradient2. I thought I read
> it was improved in the new version although I cannot see it in the dev
> version I have at the moment.

I think that to be more consistent across scales, it would be better to have something like this:
scale_colour(type="hue")
scale_colour(type="gradientn")
scale_fill(type="gradient")

This would keep the syntax parallel with your proposed scale_x(), where the part after the "scale_" is the name of the aesthetic. The 'type=' parameter could also be used for other scales. Here's one possibility:
scale_shape(type="hollow")

> scale_colour_hue is difficult to understand by novice,
> non-graphic-oriented users (particularly non-english speaking ones).
> What about scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous, to match
> with all the rest of the scales?

Don't scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous default to using hue? For example, these both give the same result:

dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=3)
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=x)) + geom_bar() + scale_fill_discrete()
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=x)) + geom_bar() + scale_fill_hue()

I agree that "hue" can be difficult to understand for novices. I also think that it is usually not a good choice, and I almost never use it. This is because lightness is kept constant, making it hard to distinguish differently-colored regions. The hues can often be difficult for colorblind people to distinguish. For example, with three hues, like in the example above, the red and green bars look very similar for those with red-green colorblindness. (I'm using a program called Sim Daltonism on my Mac to simulate what things look like for colorblind people.)

>
> Finally, the fact that "colour" affects the inside of objects for
> geom_point but the outside for most others is bad for consistency and
> hence learning and discovery. What about having separate fill and
> stroke for all geoms (with stroke basically replacing colour
> currently)? And then have colour do something "intelligent" depending
> on the scale (i.e. stroke for path, fill for polygon, fill for tile
> etc.). That would give fine, consistent control when needed
> (fill/stroke) but also allow a more natural approach ("I want this to
> be *coloured* according to that", without having to care what the
> colour is applied to). This simpler approach would probably suffice
> for the majority of users (very rarely do I use both fill and stroke
> colours on the same object).

The inconsistent meaning of 'colour' can be traced to grid graphics, specifically gpar. If you look at ?gpar, you'll see a 'col' and 'fill' parameter. The 'colour' in ggplot2 gets mapped to 'col', and 'fill' goes to 'fill'. For example, the inconsistency in the shape colour/fill specification can be traced here. The fill-only shapes (15-18) have no outline and use 'col' to refer to the fill color. The hollow shapes (0-14) are only outlines, and 'col' refers to the line color. The fill+outline shapes (21-25) use 'col' to refer to the outline, and 'fill' to refer to the fill.

Side note: It probably wouldn't be too difficult to insulate the user from this inconsistency in color/fill for shapes.

I think it would be best to use something like 'linecolour' instead of 'colour', to always refer to lines, and keep 'fill' to refer to fill colors. Various line properties could be named like this.
- linetype
- linecolour
- linesize (instead of 'size')
- lineend

These changes would definitely break backward compatibility. But it might be worthwhile.

-Winston

messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: enhancing the discovery of newly created variables
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Jan 18, 2012 at 4:11 PM, JiHO <jo.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> Enhancing the discoverability of the variables computed by stats and,
> particularly, the variables extracted by fortify would be nice.
> However, I don't have a good solution (a message would probably be
> annoying). Any suggestion is welcome.

I agree that this would be very useful. For example, if you are adding a linear regression line with stat_smooth(), it's very desirable to be able get the lm object out of ggplot. The way ggplot works right now, you have to do the lm() separately to get the numbers. This makes me feel uneasy because I'm not absolutely sure that the lm object is the same as what's on the graph.

Here's an example:

dat <- data.frame(x=rnorm(20), y=rnorm(20))
# graph
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method=lm)
# linear model
lm(y~x, data=dat)

The lm object looks right, but what if I made a small mistake that is hard to see by inspecting the lm numbers and the graph?

Perhaps one way to do this is to have a function that takes a ggplot object and returns a list of models and fortify output. Something like this:

p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method=lm) + stat_smooth()

extract_stat(p)
# Return a list with lm object, and fortify output

It could also do the same with loess or glm fits. I think this could also be extended to other stats, like stat_summary and stat_bin.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
> My point of view is: ggplot2 is still in version < 1.0, if things
> don't get broken for the sake of improvement now, they never will …
> except in a hypothetical ggplot3 but that wouldn't be a good idea.
> This is why some of the changes I suggest might be a bit radical. In
> all cases I think they would be worth it (even though I have a *lot*
> of ggplot code that would need to be updated). It would be good to
> know what other people think.

FYI I am already contemplating the idea of ggplot3, which would fix
some of what I now consider to be mistakes in the design of ggplot2.
I'm unwilling to make too many changes to ggplot2, because I don't
want to break everyone's code.

> Improving the documentation would greatly ease the discovery of
> ggplot. I used the stable version because I did not want to get into
> trouble with the dev one with students. I know lots of improvements
> are coming which is great. It might need to go a little further:
>        . detail of the statistics computed by geoms, when they do;

Much better in devel version.

>        . advice on usage such as with geom_point;

Please suggest what you want to see.

>        . more links between functions in the See Also part;

Much better in devel version.

>        . but, at the same time, better compartmentalization within the help
> of each function (i.e. do not use stuff that are potentially not yet
> known by the user).

You don't ask for much! ;)

> In particular, an homogenous syntax in the example section would be
> much welcome, at least for the first few examples of each geom. I
> understand Hadley probably wanted to mix qplot, ggplot, p <- ggplot()
> + … and all the other niceties and richness of ggplot. But that makes
> it harder to teach and understand. In geom_point (probably the first
> everyone looks at) the data and aes are specified first in ggplot and
> then in the geom call, the aesthetic call does not explicitly specify
> the arguments etc. I would suggest:
>        . use :
>                ggplot() + geom_***(mapping=aes(x=foo, y=bar), data=myD)
>        as the default notation, in full, everywhere. It is the most
> versatile (save for layer(), but that is almost never used) and the
> most consistent.
>        . then in later examples, introduce the refinements/shortcuts such as:
>                - omitting argument names
>                - specifying stuff within the ggplot() call, that will be inherited
>                - storing the plot as an object and modifying it afterwards
>                - using qplot

I think you're asking for too much from the documentation - I don't
think it's appropriate to try and teach issues like this in the
examples, you really need to consult a higher-level introduction which
points out how everything fits together.  Currently, the only place to
get this from the book, and while I would like to produce an open,
freely available, version, I currently don't have the time to write
it.  Community contributions would be greatly appreciated!

> Finally, separating "drawing geoms" (those for which stat="identify")
> and "statistical geoms" (those in which computation is made on the
> data before plotting) on the website and in the doc would help
> regarding teaching (e.g. "Start with the basics, then dive into more
> complex stuff").

This is something that I want to fix in ggplot3 - the current naming
scheme is confusing.  I'd rather have layer_histogram and geom_bar +
stat_bin, rather than the current mishmash where some geoms are real
geoms (point, line, polygon), and some are aliases for combinations of
stats and geoms (quantile, smooth, histogram).

Hadley

Technically, allowing themes to affect the data-elements would be
complex, and, I suspect, confusing (because it would become
increasingly hard to figure out why your points were blue).

> popular with design-nerds and this is an audience ggplot2 has interest
> in pleasing (they are the ones that make ggplot look good on the web)
> and almost has the means to please.

I agree that this would be nice, but I don't see any easy way of
implementing it.

messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: reorganisation and renaming of colour scales
messages.body_plain:
> Basically, scale_gradient should be the only interface, behave like
> scale_gradientn and have a midpoint argument, NULL by default, which,
> when specified, makes it behave like scale_gradient2. I thought I read
> it was improved in the new version although I cannot see it in the dev
> version I have at the moment.

If you want to use the scale gradients in that way, just use
scale_gradientn - they are now all implemented with the (mostly) the
same algorithm behind the scenes. But scale_gradient2 is a little
special because it ensures that the gradient is symmetrical around the
midpoint, even if the data are not.  I think this behaviour is
different enough to deserve its own name and it would be confusing to
lump into one scale.

> scale_colour_hue is difficult to understand by novice,
> non-graphic-oriented users (particularly non-english speaking ones).
> What about scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous, to match
> with all the rest of the scales?

Why is scale_colour_hue confusing?

> Finally, the fact that "colour" affects the inside of objects for
> geom_point but the outside for most others is bad for consistency and
> hence learning and discovery. What about having separate fill and
> stroke for all geoms (with stroke basically replacing colour
> currently)? And then have colour do something "intelligent" depending
> on the scale (i.e. stroke for path, fill for polygon, fill for tile
> etc.). That would give fine, consistent control when needed
> (fill/stroke) but also allow a more natural approach ("I want this to
> be *coloured* according to that", without having to care what the
> colour is applied to). This simpler approach would probably suffice
> for the majority of users (very rarely do I use both fill and stroke
> colours on the same object).

I guess I don't really see the problem here - I just think of points
as being all outside.  It would be possible to wrap around the default
R behaviour (which I agree is confusing), but it would require a lot
of extra work, for not much extra gain.

> I understand this would also cause a backward compatibility problem
> (using both fill and colour on something where colour would refere to
> fill) but again, that would be the price for a better behaviour in the
> end.

I think if I did it again I'd use stroke and fill.

Hadley

messages.subject_clean: Strange allignment in axis grob
messages.body_plain:
This was the fix Takahashi made for 0.89.

guide_axis <- function(at, labels, position="right", theme) {
		position <- match.arg(position, c("top", "bottom", "right", "left"))

		at <- unit(at, "native")
		length <- theme$axis.ticks.length
		label_pos <- length + theme$axis.ticks.margin
		one <- unit(1, "npc")

		label_render <- switch(position,
							   top = , bottom = "axis.text.x",
							   left = , right = "axis.text.y"
							   )
		label_x <- switch(position,
						  top = ,
						  bottom = at,
						  right = label_pos,
						  left = one - label_pos
						  )
		label_y <- switch(position,
						  top = label_pos,
						  bottom = one - label_pos,
						  right = ,
						  left = at,
						  )

		if (is.list(labels)) {
			if (any(sapply(labels, is.language))) {
				labels <- do.call(expression, labels)
			} else {
				labels <- unlist(labels)
			}
		}

		labels <- theme_render(theme, label_render, labels, label_x, label_y)

		line <- switch(position,
					   top =    theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 0, 1, 0),
					   bottom = theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 1, 1, 1),
					   right =  theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 1, 0, 1),
					   left =   theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 1, 0, 1, 1)
					   )

		ticks <- switch(position,
						top =    theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", at, 0, at, length),
						bottom = theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", at, one - length, at, 1),
						right =  theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", 0, at, length, at),
						left =   theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", one - length, at, 1, at)
						)

		absoluteGrob(
					 gList(ticks, labels, line),
					 width = grobWidth(labels) + label_pos,
					 height = grobHeight(labels) + label_pos
					 )
	}
	assignInNamespace("guide_axis",guide_axis, "ggplot2")

I agree with Hadley here.  I'm often wanting to pass fitted model
objects to geom_smooth -- for example, if I've already fitted a model,
why make ggplot fit it again?  I'm not sure how difficult this would be
to implement, but a wish of mine is to be able to pass any fitted model
object of class with a predict method (e.g. lme):

mod <- lme(y ~ x, data = dat, random = ~ x | z)
p <- ggplot(dat) + facet_wrap( ~ z) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y)) +
geom_smooth(model = mod)

I can already foresee some potential implementation issues though --
e.g. lme predictions require the specification of the level in the
hierarchical structure of the model at which predictions are to be made;
and interval estimates of lme predictions are notoriously difficult to
make (so maybe force 'se = FALSE' in geom_smooth?).  In any case, its
exciting to me that you're thinking along these lines Hadley.  I'll give
it some more thought myself, in terms of specific implementation ideas.

Steve

>> ggplot(japan_map, aes(long, lat, group=group)) + geom_path()

>> ggplot(Region, aes(long, lot)) + geom_point(aes(size = population))

You need to learn a bit more about the basics of ggplot (there's a
great book for that at a very fair price ;) ). Basically you can
supply each geom with a separate dataset and then you just "add" them:

ggplot() + geom_path(aes(x=long, y=lat, group=group), data=japan_map)
+ geom_point(aes(x=long, y=lat, size = population), data=Region)

which can even be simplified in

ggplot(mapping=aes(x=long, y=lat)) + geom_path(aes(group=group),
data=japan_map) + geom_point(aes(size = population), data=Region)

since long and lat are common to both geoms.

On Thu, Jan 19, 2012 at 14:15, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
>> Perhaps one way to do this is to have a function that takes a ggplot object
>> and returns a list of models and fortify output. Something like this:
>>
>> p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method=lm) +
>> stat_smooth()
>>
>> extract_stat(p)
>> # Return a list with lm object, and fortify output
>>
>> It could also do the same with loess or glm fits. I think this could also be
>> extended to other stats, like stat_summary and stat_bin.
>
> I'd rather make it easier to do the opposite:
>
> mod <- gam(y ~ s(x) ,data = dat)
> p  <-  ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(model = mod)
>
> I generally think it's a bad idea to rely on a graphics package to do
> your statistics for you.

I agree. And to continue on the teacher's point of view, I always
teach my students to compute the model manually and extract necessary
data from it (fitted values, residuals etc.) to make the plots.
Otherwise, they don't understand how the display of the model and the
actual modeling process are connected.

I think that ggplot can help with this data extraction part (cf
fortify) but shouldn't try to do the whole thing. A plot of the
results of the model is not enough anyway.

As for the syntax, what about

mod <- gam(y ~ s(x) ,data = dat)

ggplot(mod) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_line(aes(x=x, y=.fitted.values.))

with fortify handling the data extraction from mod behind the scenes.
This format would allow fine control and to produce any plot
imaginable. And this

autoplot(mod)
autoplot(mod, type="resid")

to produce automatically some commonly used plots (fit, residuals vs
fitted, qqplot of residuals etc.). This is the direction I took based
on your advice for factorial analysis plots. The
geom_smooth(model=mod) strikes me as kind of in-between: neither fully
automated nor giving complete control and I am not sure how it would
scale/generalize.

JiHO

>

Actually, this suggestion was a for a minor change. If a major cahnge
is to be made to the scales, there would only be scale_fill(),
scale_stroke() (and possibly scale_colour() cf my other suggestion
below) and the general type of the scale (continuous or discrete)
would be guessed from the data.

>> scale_colour_hue is difficult to understand by novice,
>> non-graphic-oriented users (particularly non-english speaking ones).
>> What about scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous, to match
>> with all the rest of the scales?
>
> Don't scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous

I just discovered that scale_colour_continuous actually exists. But
that seems to be a change in the devel version.

> default to using
> hue? For example, these both give the same result:
>
> dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=3)
> ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=x)) + geom_bar() + scale_fill_discrete()
> ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=x)) + geom_bar() + scale_fill_hue()

Yes but that are two discrete scales. This:

ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=x)) + geom_bar() + scale_fill_continuous()

does not work. i.e.
	hue = discrete
	gradient = continuous

> I agree that "hue" can be difficult to understand for novices. I also think
> that it is usually not a good choice, and I almost never use it. This is
> because lightness is kept constant, making it hard to distinguish
> differently-colored regions. The hues can often be difficult for colorblind
> people to distinguish. For example, with three hues, like in the example
> above, the red and green bars look very similar for those with red-green
> colorblindness. (I'm using a program called Sim Daltonism on my Mac to
> simulate what things look like for colorblind people.)

That's probably what scale_brewer is for. But finding a good set of
colours which satisfy several conditions (color blindness,
projector-proof, copiable etc.) is hard. And actually, there are not
that many sets, even in ColorBrewer, with more than 4 colours that
satisfy these conditions.

Given this and because scale_fill/colour_discrete can require an
arbitrary number of colours, using evenly spaced hues makes sense even
if that's not the absolute best choice.

>> Finally, the fact that "colour" affects the inside of objects for
>> geom_point but the outside for most others is bad for consistency and
>> hence learning and discovery.
>

> The inconsistent meaning of 'colour' can be traced to grid graphics,
> specifically gpar. If you look at ?gpar, you'll see a 'col' and 'fill'
> parameter. The 'colour' in ggplot2 gets mapped to 'col', and 'fill' goes to
> 'fill'. For example, the inconsistency in the shape colour/fill
> specification can be traced here. The fill-only shapes (15-18) have no
> outline and use 'col' to refer to the fill color. The hollow shapes (0-14)
> are only outlines, and 'col' refers to the line color. The fill+outline
> shapes (21-25) use 'col' to refer to the outline, and 'fill' to refer to the
> fill.

OK, thanks for the pointer.

> Side note: It probably wouldn't be too difficult to insulate the user from
> this inconsistency in color/fill for shapes.

Indeed, that's what I was thinking of.

> I think it would be best to use something like 'linecolour' instead of
> 'colour', to always refer to lines, and keep 'fill' to refer to fill colors.
> Various line properties could be named like this.
> - linetype
> - linecolour

Isn't "stroke" generic enough. But maybe that is, like hue, a too
technical term.

> - linesize (instead of 'size')

But size applies to several other things (points, etc.)

JiHO

> scale_gradientn - they are now all implemented with the (mostly) the
> same algorithm behind the scenes.

Indeed (and that's what I do), but exposing all three (on the website,
in the documentation, in examples) complexifies the situation,
needlessly I would argue. Isn't it possible to keep them around for
backward compatibility sake (since they are based on about the same
code, they wouldn't require too much additional maintenance) but only
expose scale_colour/fill_gradient (or actually
scale_colour/fill_continuous... or even actually scale_colour/fill ;)
)

> But scale_gradient2 is a little
> special because it ensures that the gradient is symmetrical around the
> midpoint, even if the data are not.  I think this behaviour is
> different enough to deserve its own name and it would be confusing to
> lump into one scale.

OK. I think that a midpoint argument with the explanation of the
behaviour in the documentation would have been enough but that's
probably just a question of taste. I usually prefer having a
seemlingly simple interface at first approach that "hides" more
complex behaviours up its sleeve (e.g. in OS X, I find the menu items
that change when `alt` is pressed genius: the functionality is there
for advanced users who look for it but it does not clutter the
interface).

>> scale_colour_hue is difficult to understand by novice,
>> non-graphic-oriented users (particularly non-english speaking ones).

Because most people don't know what "hue" is ;)

> as being all outside.  It would be possible to wrap around the default
> R behaviour (which I agree is confusing), but it would require a lot
> of extra work, for not much extra gain.

I actually think of hollow shapes as being all outside and filled ones
as being all inside, so the default points of ggplot are all inside to
me ;)
But, anyway some shapes of "points" have both inside and outside and
those would require separate control. I think they would actually be
the best default, with by default, only fill, because they are most
similar to other shapes and the most versatile.

I encountered a situation a little while ago where having both fill
and stroke for points would have been useful. I actually asked the
question to the list and there was no solution (except using another
aesthetic to map the variable I wanted to map to the stroke).

>> What about having separate fill and
>> stroke for all geoms (with stroke basically replacing colour
>> currently)? And then have colour do something "intelligent" depending
>> on the scale (i.e. stroke for path, fill for polygon, fill for tile
>> etc.). That would give fine, consistent control when needed
>> (fill/stroke) but also allow a more natural approach ("I want this to

And it is too late for that? :-(

OK. Being able to change the font with one line of code is indeed
necessary and your way is much more versatile and clever than my
suggestion of using using base_family, base_size etc.
But you could mix the content of those elements however you want? Such as:

	theme$text = list(size = 12, family = "Helvetica")
	theme$y = list(angle = 90)
	theme$axis.text = list(size = 10)

	theme$x = list(size = 15)

In that case, how would you decide on the size of the text on the x
axis? Does axis.text take precedence or x?

>> This also means that users would have access to each element of the
>> current theme and do things like "annotate the plot with a vertical
>> line *the same colour as the current grid*". And this would work even
>> when the whole theme is changed and the grid becomes black for

>
> It's not obvious to me how that would work.  Within a geom, you'd need
> some way of delaying evaluation of the aesthetic until the plot was
> rendered.  This tends to be complex and bug-prone.

I did not think about the technical aspect of this of course. But
currently, the theme used by a plot is the one that was in place when
the plot was *constructed*, not when the plot is rendered, right? This
would be the same: at the time the plot is constructed, fetch the
current grid colour and use that in the layer of the plot.

By "this would work even when the whole theme is changed" I don't mean
changing the theme on the fly, I mean writing some code with the
default theme, realizing the journal/presentation requires something
else and regenerating the plots with a new theme.
Currently, if we keep the example of the grid colour I could do

	d = data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10)-0.5)
	ggplot(d) +
		geom_hline(yintercept=0, size=2, colour="white") +
	    geom_point(aes(x, y))

to emphasize 0 in the y direction. Now if I do:

	theme_set(theme_bw(12))
	d = data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10)-0.5)
	ggplot(d) +
		geom_hline(yintercept=0, size=2, colour="white") +
	    geom_point(aes(x, y))

this does not work anymore, I must change it to:

	ggplot(d) +
		geom_hline(yintercept=0, size=2, colour="grey30") +
		geom_point(aes(x, y))

What I would have preferred to write would have been something like:

	ggplot(d) +
		geom_hline(yintercept=0, size=2, colour=theme$major$colour) +
		geom_point(aes(x, y))

>> Combined with adding constants to the list such as the existing:
>>        . base_size
>>        . base_family
>> but also
>>        . base_fill
>>        . base_stroke

>
> See above, but themes are explicitly tied to non-data elements.
> Technically, allowing themes to affect the data-elements would be
> complex,

I probably have a very bad idea of how these things work internally
but, assuming that my reasonning above is correct (theme is evaluted
when the plot is built), using something like
theme$base_fill/stroke/colour (or theme$content_colour) as the default
in all geoms would simply get replaced by the content of this variable
(which is ensured to exist because a theme is loaded when ggplot is
loaded) when the plot is built. And then this would be rendered as any
other colour.

> and, I suspect, confusing (because it would become
> increasingly hard to figure out why your points were blue).

I see where you are going with the possible confusion, theoretically.
But I don't think it would be very different, in the end, to setting
colour="blue" in the geom call, and that does not seem to be a
problem.

Currently points are black on a grey background and this is natural
because black and grey aren't really colours. But I think that blue
points on a blue background would give the same impression. See this
for an example
	http://dl.dropbox.com/u/1047321/ggplot/Screen%20Shot%202012-01-19%20at%2023.46.08%20.png

>> For example, if I want all plots to have a blue-ish aspect to fit with
>> the design of a given piece of work, I can change the grid background

>> in pleasing (they are the ones that make ggplot look good on the web)
>> and almost has the means to please.

> implementing it.

Again, I thought that having a defaut colour in the theme that would
exist before any plot is created and be evaluated when the plot is
built would work. When it would come to displaying the plot the colour
would be already coded as "#4A88FE" and not theme$base_colour anymore.
But of course it might be (probably is) more complicated.
