>> My point of view is: ggplot2 is still in version < 1.0, if things
>> don't get broken for the sake of improvement now, they never will …
>

> FYI I am already contemplating the idea of ggplot3, which would fix
> some of what I now consider to be mistakes in the design of ggplot2.

OK. Something re-coded in a different language, as you mentioned a
while ago? Recoding from scratch always opens great opportunities but
I don't know where you find the time and energy for all this (I am
just immensely grateful you do!).
I will continue offering internships for math/IT engineering students
with the hope that R and ggplot will eventually attract someone but
such a overhaul of the project is likely to be something that only you
can do, right?

> I'm unwilling to make too many changes to ggplot2, because I don't
> want to break everyone's code.

:(
As I said, I have a *lot* of legacy ggplot2 code but I would be OK
with rewriting some of it to account for streamlining and improvements
in ggplot2. Given the version number, the pace at which ggplot is
evolving... and the bugginess of some of its components I must admit
;) , I always assumed that it was still in an experimental phase and
that fixing my code from time to time was the price to pay for
something as powerful, innovative and dynamic.

It would be nice to know what other people on this list think.

>> Improving the documentation

>>        . advice on usage such as with geom_point;
>
> Please suggest what you want to see.

I am not an expert in data representation, and surely the
documentation of R functions is not the place for detailled
explanations or copy-pasting from books. But a few sentences, gathered
from your experience and literature review, explaining things such as:
- why scaling area rather than diameter is better perceptually for points
- in what conditions using a barplot makes sense (it starts from 0)
and suggest that, in many cases where people use barplots, a boxplot
might be more appropriate
- a bit of the history of boxplots, what the symbols represent in this
implementation (even though it should be standard, it isn't)
- why using more than 5-6 colours along a hue scale is not a good idea
perceptually
- how colour scales based on hue only can cause problems (see earlier
discussion about constant luminance)
- why a grey background and light grid is better than the opposite (in
the theme documentation)
etc.

>> In particular, an homogenous syntax in the example section would be

>> much welcome, at least for the first few examples of each geom.[...]

>> I would suggest:
>>        . use :
>>                ggplot() + geom_***(mapping=aes(x=foo, y=bar), data=myD)
>>        as the default notation, in full, everywhere. It is the most
>> versatile (save for layer(), but that is almost never used) and the
>> most consistent.
>>        . then in later examples, introduce the refinements/shortcuts such as:
>>                - omitting argument names
>>                - specifying stuff within the ggplot() call, that will be inherited
>>                - storing the plot as an object and modifying it afterwards
>>                - using qplot
>
> I think you're asking for too much from the documentation - I don't
> think it's appropriate to try and teach issues like this in the
> examples, you really need to consult a higher-level introduction which
> points out how everything fits together.  Currently, the only place to
> get this from the book, and while I would like to produce an open,
> freely available, version, I currently don't have the time to write
> it.

I know I am asking for more than what is currently available in the
ggplot documentation but I don't think it would be too much to ask of
it. Other packages provide quite detailed documentation (see
quantreg::rq for example, or stats::p.adjust): the documentation goes
well further what is technically needed to the get the function to
run.

The first reference for ggplot newcomers is the documentation
(actually, probably the website, but it is the same). So I think it
would be a good place to teach ggplot2 (and graphical representation
of data) a little.
If not, then at least the examples should be formated with a
consistent and robust syntax. Because, currently, one could have
trouble understanding how scale_size works for example, simply because
he/she does not know about qplot(), last_plot(), the fact that you can
save a plot into an object and later modify it, etc. which are all
exclusively used in the examples. This would defeat the purpose of the
documentation and the examples.

> Community contributions would be greatly appreciated!

In the form of vignette(s)?

JiHO

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Jan 19, 2012 at 13:56, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
>>> The homogeneity between the arguments of all the scales (name, breaks,
>>> labels, etc.) would justify and ease the use of these "higher level"
>>> functions. Of course some arguments are specific and the continuous
>>> and discrete cases should be distinguished in the help but having
>>> these simpler more "intelligent" functions as the main front end would
>>> be way better I think.
>>
>> I agree that from a user perspective, it would be much simpler to not
>> specify continuous vs. discrete, since that's already determined by the
>> data. Perhaps someone with more experience programming the scales would like
>> to comment on whether this is technically feasible?
>
> I don't think it is - ggplot2 can only know the type of the scale when
> the plotted is rendered, not when the scale is added.  This means that
> if you specified incorrect arguments you wouldn't find out until quite
> late, and it would be confusing as to where the error came from.

Too bad. So it means that, when the plot is constructed, ggplot has no
way of checking the type of the data associated with x/y/colour/...?

Indeed, I can remark that:

	d <- data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10), z=rep(c("a", "b"), 5))
	ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z)) + scale_colour_gradient("foo")

throws an error but

	p <- ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z)) +
scale_colour_gradient("foo")

works. Only when I do

	print(p)

do I get the error.

Is it a design principle? A consequence of the tools that are used to
construct ggplots (proto and the like)? Is that something that could
be changed (because beyond the proposed change, having the error thown
in the second example above would be much more valuable than at
rendering time).

> While I appreciate the importance of easily typed functions, I have
> gradually been moving to make ggplot2 more explicit and verbose as
> that seems to cause less confusion overall.

It is more about easily understood than easily typed. The type of
scale is determined by the data, so writing
	scale_x_*continuous*
when the data is a bunch of numbers seems redundant, is harder to
learn, and suggests that is is possible to use a different type of x
scale for this same data, when it isn't.

NB: Actually, these work
	d <- data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10))
	ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z)) +
scale_x_discrete(breaks=c(0,0.5,1))
	ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z)) + scale_x_date()
but do not produce at all what is expected. They should probably
rather throw an error.

If there are situations where the different scales can be applied to
the same data type, then there is additional value in, and a
justification for, specifying the type of scale everytime. But I can't
think of any right now. That's why I find it difficult to explain why
the _continuous/_discrete sufixes even exist.

Depending on your answer regarding technical feasability, I'll be
happy to draft a more complete plan for these higher level scales,
trying to consider all (documented at least) scales.

PS: Is that something that is implemented in the scales package or is
`scales` more about where to put the breaks and this kind of stuff?

JiHO

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Jan 19, 2012 at 13:55, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
> See the discussion here:
>
> https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/161 and here
> https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/82

Yeah, that's me again.

> * there are two types of bar charts and unfortunately we give them the
> same name.  It's equally valid to expect that geom_bar will produce
> either of them
>
> * Unless you can provide compelling evidence that one is much more
> common that the other,

I cannot provide general, literature-based evidence but I can say that
every single student I've taught:
- uses geom_histogram rather than geom_bar when asked to "represent
the distribution of a piece of data"
- is puzzled by the behaviour of geom_bar when he/she first tries it
I know this for a fact because these are two necessary steps in the
labs they do with me.

I insist that the first question does not mention the word "histogram"
but just "distribution" (because I would also accept a density plot),
but histogram is what they naturally think of and when they search the
documentation for it, they find geom_histogram.
The second question is about the total abundance of several species in
a dataset in three different locations, so they are usually drawn
towards a bar chart with three bars of different colour per species
(Excel habits I guess). Which either throws an error when the don't
pre-compute the sum of abundances or works (but abusively IMHO -- see
previous email) when they do.

> or suggest better names for both, I'm unwilling
> to change the current behaviour because I think it will cause just as
> many problems (but in the other direction)

I don't think the names could be improved (certainly not
geom_histogram and I can't think of something else for geom_bar).
But an additional argument to keep those names but change the
behaviour might be that:
- barplot() in base R produces bars of specified height (i.e. as
geom_bar with stat="identity")
- hist() in base R produces a histogram

It would be good to have the opinion of a larger sample of people on
this matter. Thanks in advance,

JiHO

> OK. Being able to change the font with one line of code is indeed

>        theme$x = list(size = 15)
>
> In that case, how would you decide on the size of the text on the x
> axis? Does axis.text take precedence or x?

Yeah, the the challenge would be getting the precedence rules right.
In this case I think it's simple - axis.text would take precedence
because it's more specific.  A more challenging example would be

theme$axis.text = list(size = 10)

theme$text.x = list(size = 12)
theme$axis.x = list(size = 14)

which is rather contrived, but we'd still need a general rule to
handle it.  Maybe something like: the if the theme item is
axis.text.x, then axis would get 4 points, text 2 points and x 1.
Rules would be applied in reverse order of their points, so that
axis.text.x would have the highest precedence, followed by axis.text,
then axis.x, then text.x.  Order of elements wouldn't matter.

> I did not think about the technical aspect of this of course. But
> currently, the theme used by a plot is the one that was in place when
> the plot was *constructed*, not when the plot is rendered, right? This
> would be the same: at the time the plot is constructed, fetch the
> current grid colour and use that in the layer of the plot.

Nope:

p <- qplot(mpg, wt, data = mtcars)
ggtheme(theme_bw())
p

> else and regenerating the plots with a new theme.

Which you can basically do already, with get("colour",

Yes, but it doesn't work that way :/

> construct ggplots (proto and the like)? Is that something that could
> be changed (because beyond the proposed change, having the error thown
> in the second example above would be much more valuable than at
> rendering time).

No - because there are so many ways of creating a plot:

d <- data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10), z=rep(c("a", "b"), 5))

ggplot(d) + scale_colour_gradient("foo") + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z))
ggplot() + scale_colour_gradient("foo") + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y,
colour=z)) %+% d
ggplot(d) + scale_colour_gradient("foo") + aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z) +
geom_point()

and every possible permutation of those.  This is a key part of the
flexibility of ggplot2 - you are not constrained to build up the plot
in a certain way.

>> gradually been moving to make ggplot2 more explicit and verbose as

> If there are situations where the different scales can be applied to

> think of any right now. That's why I find it difficult to explain why
> the _continuous/_discrete sufixes even exist.

What about the fact the continuous and discrete scales behave in
completely different ways? And have different arguments? Or you
haven't yet put any data on the plot? If you don't know whether your

>

> Maybe I'll give it a shot over the weekend. (I'll probably post progress to

That seems like exactly what fortify is meant for. You probably should
wrap this into a method for fortify and follow its convention in
naming the variables (preprend a dot "." for extracted variables). See
fortify.lm() as an example.

> One thing I'm not sure about is how to deal with aesthetic mappings. Say you
> have a factor mapped to colour and want to add model lines for each one. You
> could add each one separately and manually set the color, but this seems
> clunky. I guess maybe you put the model objects in a list somehow, but you'd
> also have to preserve information about the factor(s) levels that each model
> object corresponds to. I don't see a really good way to do this. Thoughts?

I think that the "correct" way to do this would be to have the factor
in the model in a way that affects both the intercept and slope (i.e.
fit one separate model per factor level, but do this in one model
call) and then use this in ggplot. Example:

    set.seed(123)
    x <- runif(20, 0, 10)
    a <- factor(rep(c("foo", "bar"), each=10))
    y <- x*(0.5*as.numeric(a)) + (3+as.numeric(a)) + runif(20, 0, 3)
    d <- data.frame(x, y, a)
    library("ggplot2")
    ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, colour=a))

    m <- lm(y ~ x + a + a:x, data=d)
    df <- fortify(m)
    ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, colour=a)) + geom_point() +
geom_line(aes(y=.fitted))

Is that what you meant?

JiHO

I am not sure I understand what you mean here.

What I meant by "do not produce what is expected" is that, in the
stable version, the two examples above produce a plot with points at
the same location but with no x axis.
In the devel version there is an x axis but which is strangely formed:

    d <- data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10))
    ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y))
    ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y)) + scale_x_discrete(breaks=c(0,0.5,1))
    # produces a axis with breaks at 0 and 1 only and leaves a lot of
blank space on the right of 1
    ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y)) + scale_x_date()
    # produces an axis whose breaks depend on the current time (apparently)

In both cases I don't understand what they would be used for.

>> If there are situations where the different scales can be applied to
>> the same data type, then there is additional value in, and a
>> justification for, specifying the type of scale everytime. But I can't
>> think of any right now. That's why I find it difficult to explain why
>> the _continuous/_discrete sufixes even exist.
>
> What about the fact the continuous and discrete scales behave in
> completely different ways?

I agree they should, but the interface is still similar (both have
name, breaks, labels etc.). My question is whether ggplot can decide
which one to use on its own everytime or whether it needs the user to
specify it explicitly.
My impression is that ggplot would have enough information by looking
at the class of the data associated with the scale. Now that may be a
technical impossibility (cf above, the fact that the data is sometimes
known only at render time).

> And have different arguments?

Many are common though:
discrete            continuous

aesthetics          aesthetics
scale_name          scale_name
palette             palette
name = NULL         name = NULL
breaks = NULL       breaks = NULL
                    minor_breaks = NULL
labels = NULL       labels = NULL
legend = NULL       legend = NULL
limits = NULL       limits = NULL
                    rescaler = rescale
                    oob = censor
expand = c(0,0)     expand = c(0, 0)
na.value = NA       na.value = NA
drop = TRUE
                    trans = "identity"
guide = "legend"    guide = "legend"

So documenting them in a single function and explain only the
differences would probably be easy.

> Or you
> haven't yet put any data on the plot?

That's indeed something I did not think about. Cf. your examples above.

> If you don't know whether your
> data is continuous or discrete you have bigger problems?

I'm not saying it is hard for the user to know wether its data is
discrete or continuous (or a date, or ...). I'm saying that it seems
like it wouldn't be hard for ggplot to figure it out and spare the
user having to think about it and write it explicitly. The whole
concept of scales is difficult to apprehend for newcomers so anything
that makes it more fluid, more intuitive seems very valuable to me.
having to write _continuous or _discrete at the end of the scale name
costs more than the few keystrokes it requires.

>> Depending on your answer regarding technical feasability, I'll be
>> happy to draft a more complete plan for these higher level scales,
>> trying to consider all (documented at least) scales.

> I'd recommend working your way through build.r to better understand
> the process by which the plot is built up.

Will do (again! ;) maybe after a few times I'll understand it completely).

This stems for what I observed to be the natural behaviour of
newcomers when they discover a new ggplot function (a geom let us
say): they read the description, skim over the syntax, check which
arguments are mandatory and what aesthetics can be mapped and then
jump to the examples. They run a few and when they feel they have what
they need, copy-paste the example and adapt it to their data. Later
when they need to do finer things with the function, they come back to
the documentation, read it a bit more in depth, and run a few more
examples.

It is not the canonical way to learn but is quite natural, "organic"
and it is actually quite efficient with most R functions, even beyond
of ggplot. It will never replace reading a book or taking a class but
it helps progressing little by little, by practicing, without having
to do all the hard learning up-front.

>>> Community contributions would be greatly appreciated!
>>

>
> In any form!  (especially as github pull requests)

;) I'll try to make these documentation changes on a few geoms, as
unobtrusively as possible and you'll let me know what you think.
(NB: don't expect them immediately though, it's grand proposal time now ! )

JiHO

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I don't agree with your premise that geom_bar() and geom_histogram()
do the 'exact same thing'. This is a common misperception. Bar charts
are meant to visualize discrete distributions; a histogram is a crude
type of density estimator with (when correctly used) a fixed bandwidth
(i.e., binwidth) and a uniform kernel function. There's a good reason
why that little space between categories in a bar chart exists - it
signifies that the values are not meant to be interpreted on a
continuous numeric scale. Similarly, the adjacency of the bars in a
histogram is a subtle visual cue that the variable of interest is on a
continuous scale. What does a bar chart mean in Europe that does not
conform to this definition?

Dennis

Yes, but you do have to please MATLAB switchers before telling them
that their jet colours are crap ;)

On a more general note, scale_gradientn with 2 colours =
scale_gradient; so scale_gradientn can do what scale_gradient does but
can also do more. Why not provide it as the sole interface with two
colours as default? Why provide a "crippled" version of it?

>> that change when `alt` is pressed genius: the functionality is there
>> for advanced users who look for it but it does not clutter the
>> interface).
>

midpoint = NULL, midpoint =NA
This would be the default.

> How does

> you even preserve symmetry in the same way?

Uh, indeed, that's something I did not realize. My bad. I would indeed
make it more difficult to integrate into scale_colour_gradient.

>>> Why is scale_colour_hue confusing?
>>
>> Because most people don't know what "hue" is ;)
>
> That's going to make it hard to come up with any good name!

scale_colour_discrete would do. basically just reverse the role of
scale_colour_discrete (becomes the main interface) and
scale_colour_hue (still valid but only mentioned in the documentation
of scale_colour_discrete).

To recap, guessing the type of scale from the type of data is
technically difficult and might induce clutter and confusion in the
documentation so you are not willing to change in this direction. Am I
correct?

Then some more minor changes could still improve a bit the consistency
of the user interface. What about using:

scale_colour_discrete		in place of scale_colour_hue
scale_colour_continuous		in place of scale_colour_gradientn and
scale_colour_gradient, and default to the new legend type by Koshke
which better represents the continuty of the scale.
scale_colour_diverging		in place of scale_colour_gradient2 (with the
same new legend). It differentiates it from gradients and is more
explicit.

which finally brings us to a new scale_colour_sequential for ordered
factors and integers with a small number of unique values. This would
be a gradient but with a limited number of stops, represented with the
usual colour-squares legend.

I am not suggesting to discard the other functions, just to "hide"
them (like scale_colour_discrete is "hidden" now).

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Jan 21, 2012 at 00:35, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I don't agree with your premise that geom_bar() and geom_histogram()
> do the 'exact same thing'.

In ggplot they do. That's what I meant:

	library("ggplot2")
	d <- data.frame(x=runif(20), y=runif(20), z=factor(round(runif(20, 0, 4))))
	ggplot(d, aes(x=x)) + geom_bar()
	ggplot(d, aes(x=x)) + geom_histogram()

	ggplot(d, aes(x=z)) + geom_bar()
	ggplot(d, aes(x=z)) + geom_histogram()

	# and the problematic cases
	ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_bar()
	ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_bar(stat="identity")
	ggplot(d, aes(x=z, y=y)) + geom_bar(colour="red") # not sure what is
done here...
	ggplot(d, aes(x=z, y=y)) + geom_bar(stat="identity", colour="red")

> This is a common misperception. Bar charts
> are meant to visualize discrete distributions; a histogram is a crude
> type of density estimator with (when correctly used) a fixed bandwidth
> (i.e., binwidth) and a uniform kernel function. There's a good reason
> why that little space between categories in a bar chart exists - it
> signifies that the values are not meant to be interpreted on a
> continuous numeric scale. Similarly, the adjacency of the bars in a
> histogram is a subtle visual cue that the variable of interest is on a
> continuous scale.

In that case, geom_bar should only allow discrete x and
geom_histogram, continuous x. That would indeed make for a clean
separation between the two. But both would still use stat="bin" by
default.

> What does a bar chart mean in Europe that does not
> conform to this definition?

I wouldn't go as far as saying that this is the "European" definition
but the definition I most commonly see is purely geometric: a bar
chart is a char with bars on it (which start from 0 on well formed
ones). But these bars can be used to display the number of occurrences
of a category (i.e. a distribution) or just any, possibly continuous,
quantity. This is the way Excel does bar charts I think: it allows to
use bars in the same way points or a line would be used.

In this later case, I think that boxplots are almost always better
suited but some people insist on drawing bars, because it highlights
that the quantity rises from 0 or simply because it's customary. In a
recent paper the main authors insisted that I drew bars + error bars
for average + SD concentrations of chemical components, even though
that was a very crude representation of the variability (and the data
was far from normal so the meaning of the mean was dubious). But that
was what they usually saw in the journal they intended to publish in.

Again, I would not agree that this is the correct definition. Yours
appears much more solid. Mine is probably just an operational
derivative of the bar chart.

JiHO

messages.body_plain:
Actually, my previous suggestions where unnecessarily complex to the
point of being silly. Just subset your data, it'll be much easier:

    library(ggplot2)
    library(reshape)

    ## Say I have correlation matrix like this one
    A <- array(c(0.1, NA, 0.3, NA, 0.4, 0.5, 0.3, NA, 0.4, 0.5), dim=c(4,4))
    m <- melt(A)

    ggplot(m, aes(X1, X2, fill = value)) +
        geom_tile() +
        scale_fill_gradient2() +
        geom_text(data=m[is.na <http://is.na>(m$value),], label="NA")

    ggplot(m, aes(X1, X2)) +
        geom_tile(aes(fill = value)) +
        scale_fill_gradient2() +
        geom_point(data=m[is.na <http://is.na>(m$value),])

And you could even do something that usually is a mistake (mapping an
aesthetic to a single value, instead of setting it) to get a legend

    ggplot(m, aes(X1, X2)) +
        geom_tile(aes(fill = value)) +
        scale_fill_gradient2() +
        geom_point(aes(size=1), data=m[is.na <http://is.na>(m$value),]) +
        scale_size(name="", to=c(3,3), breaks=1, label="NA")

but that is really devious.

I think I prefer the most straightforward one (geom_text) but if your
matrix is large then maybe points will turn out to be more elegant.

On Fri, Jan 20, 2012 at 4:11 PM, JiHO <jo.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Fri, Jan 20, 2012 at 17:55, Winston Chang <winsto...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I have some code that takes a model object and generates a data frame that
> > you then use with geom_line(). Here's roughly how it's used:
> >   pline <- predictdf( lm(y ~ x, data=dat) )
> >   ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + geom_line(data=pline)
> >
> > It probably wouldn't be hard to adapt geom_smooth/stat_smooth to do this...
> > Maybe I'll give it a shot over the weekend. (I'll probably post progress to
> > the ggplot2-dev list instead of this one.)
>
> That seems like exactly what fortify is meant for. You probably should
> wrap this into a method for fortify and follow its convention in
> naming the variables (preprend a dot "." for extracted variables). See
> fortify.lm() as an example.

The way I did it uses predict(), so it worked with any model object that has a predict() S3 method. These include lm, glm, loess, and so on. I think fortify, as currently written, needs to be customized for each type of model. However, it might be possible to have the default fortify method use predict().

>
> > One thing I'm not sure about is how to deal with aesthetic mappings. Say you
> > have a factor mapped to colour and want to add model lines for each one. You
> > could add each one separately and manually set the color, but this seems
> > clunky. I guess maybe you put the model objects in a list somehow, but you'd
> > also have to preserve information about the factor(s) levels that each model
> > object corresponds to. I don't see a really good way to do this. Thoughts?
>
> I think that the "correct" way to do this would be to have the factor
> in the model in a way that affects both the intercept and slope (i.e.
> fit one separate model per factor level, but do this in one model
> call) and then use this in ggplot. Example:
>
>    set.seed(123)
>    x <- runif(20, 0, 10)
>    a <- factor(rep(c("foo", "bar"), each=10))
>    y <- x*(0.5*as.numeric(a)) + (3+as.numeric(a)) + runif(20, 0, 3)
>    d <- data.frame(x, y, a)
>    library("ggplot2")
>    ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, colour=a))
>
>    m <- lm(y ~ x + a + a:x, data=d)
>    df <- fortify(m)
>    ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, colour=a)) + geom_point() +
> geom_line(aes(y=.fitted))
>
> Is that what you meant?

Yes, thanks -- this makes perfect sense.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Jan 21, 2012 at 23:55, Winston Chang <winsto...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> That seems like exactly what fortify is meant for. You probably should
>> wrap this into a method for fortify and follow its convention in
>> naming the variables (preprend a dot "." for extracted variables). See
>> fortify.lm() as an example.
>
>
> The way I did it uses predict(), so it worked with any model object that has
> a predict() S3 method. These include lm, glm, loess, and so on. I think
> fortify, as currently written, needs to be customized for each type of
> model. However, it might be possible to have the default fortify method use
> predict().

Indeed fortify requires a method for each type of model, but that's
probably because it extract more than just the fit. fortify.lm uses
predict though:

fortify.lm
function (model, data = model$model, ...)
{
    infl <- influence(model, do.coef = FALSE)
    data$.hat <- infl$hat
    data$.sigma <- infl$sigma
    data$.cooksd <- cooks.distance(model, infl)
    data$.fitted <- predict(model)
    data$.resid <- resid(model)
    data$.stdresid <- rstandard(model, infl)
    data
}

Maybe the code above is valid for more than just lm. In which case
maybe it should be called something like fortify.regression and
fortify.lm, fortify.glm, fortify.loess would just be aliases. From the
documentation, lm and glm would be OK but loess probably not.

The default fortify method is currently just a fallback which gives an
error message:

function (model, data, ...)
{
    stop("ggplot2 doesn't know how to deal with data of class ",
        class(model), call. = FALSE)
}

so I don't think it would be appropriate to have default actions
there. In addition, fortify can be applied to stuff other than the
result of a regression model (maps etc.) and predict does not make
sense in these other contexts.

JiHO

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Is this what you were after?

stagevals <- c('s', 'sm', 'm', 'l')
tmp <- data.frame( stage = factor(rep(stagevals, each = 3), levels = stagevals),
                            stageNum = rep(1:4, each = 3),
                            mean = c(0,0.01250000, 0.05590062,
0.02857143, 3.98437500,
                                           8.48603352, 6.51162791,
20.28571429, 1.13793103,
                                           2.81395349, 9.77192982, 20.27450980),
                            se = c(0.00000000, 0.01250000, 0.02372272,
0.02857143,
                                      0.78729331, 1.44849337,
1.23167767, 12.04893650,
                                      0.79982162, 0.72676252,
1.27076721, 4.32594348),
                           tsb = rep(15:17, each = 4),
                           tsbf = factor(rep(15:17, each = 4))
ggplot(tmp, aes(x = stage, y = mean, shape = tsbf)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_linerange(aes(ymax = mean + se, ymin = mean - se),
                   size = 1, position = "dodge")  +
    geom_line(aes(group = tsbf)) +
    scale_shape_manual(breaks = levels(tmp$tsbf),
                                    values = 15:17)

A couple of points:

(i) There is no aesthetic named pch in ggplot2; that comes from base
graphics. The equivalent in ggplot2 is shape (as in character shape),
which can only be mapped to a factor. Therefore, it will work if you
map shape to tsbf but not to tsb, which is numeric. An error will be
thrown if you map shape to a numeric variable.
(ii) When you have a factor as the x-variable and you want to plot a
mean line across the x-levels, you need to use the group = argument.
For a single line that averages across all groups, group = 1 will do.
For separate lines at each level of a factor A, use group = A. In the
above code, the grouping variable is tsbf.
(iii) When the legend doesn't quite work out as you expected, the
safety valve is to use scale_aesthetic_type(), where in this case the
aesthetic is shape and the type is manual. By specifying values =
15:17 in the call, it means that shape 15 will be mapped to level 15
of tmp$tsbf, shape 16 to level 16 and shape 17 to level 17. The
'manual' part means that you get to specify certain parts of the
legend:
    *  the breaks = argument represents the set of breaks you want to
use; in this case, we want the breaks to be the levels of tmp$tsbf;
    *  the values = argument represents the set of values to map to
breaks (i.e., a 1-1 association);
    *  the labels = argument represents the labels to associate with
the breaks; by default, they are the breaks themselves.
In this legend, the values are represented as plotting character
shapes and the labels are the levels of tmp$tsbf.

One problem with your plot is that the error bars overlap for levels
16 and 17 of tsbf at the highest level of stage (l). One way to
massage that problem is to map color to levels of tsbf as well, but it
helps to be smart about the colors you choose. Here's the default
addition of color to the plot:

ggplot(tmp, aes(x = stage, y = mean, shape = tsbf, colour = tsbf)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_linerange(aes(ymax = mean + se, ymin = mean - se),
                   size = 1, position = "dodge")  +
    geom_line(aes(group = tsbf)) +
    scale_shape_manual(breaks = levels(tmp$tsbf),
                       values = 15:17)

It's hard to distinguish the blue and green colors, so define the
color green to the lowest level, blue to the middle level (since it's
the one with the large SE) and orange to the high level. We implement
this with scale_colour_manual():

last_plot() + scale_colour_manual(breaks = levels(tmp$tsbf),
                                                  values = c('green',
'blue', 'orange'))

It's not perfect, but it's an improvement...

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
The issue is that the factor stage has different internal numbering
that is preserved when ordered. Thus, for the example that Dennis gave
order was S,SM,M,L = 1,2,3,4, when I created the dataset order was
3,4,2,1, so L is plot on the left, M next, etc.

Is there a way around this without recreating the dataset?

> >     geom_point(size = 3) +

> >                    size = 1, position = "dodge")  +
> >     geom_line(aes(group = tsbf)) +
> >     scale_shape_manual(breaks = levels(tmp$tsbf),
> >                                     values = 15:17)
>
> > A couple of points:
>
> > (i) There is no aesthetic named pch in ggplot2; that comes from base
> > graphics. The equivalent in ggplot2 is shape (as in character shape),
> > which can only be mapped to a factor. Therefore, it will work if you
> > map shape to tsbf but not to tsb, which is numeric. An error will be
> > thrown if you map shape to a numeric variable.
> > (ii) When you have a factor as the x-variable and you want to plot a
> > mean line across the x-levels, you need to use the group = argument.
> > For a single line that averages across all groups, group = 1 will do.
> > For separate lines at each level of a factor A, use group = A. In the
> > above code, the grouping variable is tsbf.

> > aesthetic is shape and the type is manual. By specifying values =
> > 15:17 in the call, it means that shape 15 will be mapped to level 15
> > of tmp$tsbf, shape 16 to level 16 and shape 17 to level 17. The
> > 'manual' part means that you get to specify certain parts of the
> > legend:
> >     *  the breaks = argument represents the set of breaks you want to
> > use; in this case, we want the breaks to be the levels of tmp$tsbf;
> >     *  the values = argument represents the set of values to map to
> > breaks (i.e., a 1-1 association);
> >     *  the labels = argument represents the labels to associate with
> > the breaks; by default, they are the breaks themselves.
> > In this legend, the values are represented as plotting character
> > shapes and the labels are the levels of tmp$tsbf.

> > 16 and 17 of tsbf at the highest level of stage (l). One way to

> > helps to be smart about the colors you choose. Here's the default
> > addition of color to the plot:

> > ggplot(tmp, aes(x = stage, y = mean, shape = tsbf, colour = tsbf)) +
> >     geom_point(size = 3) +
> >     geom_linerange(aes(ymax = mean + se, ymin = mean - se),
> >                    size = 1, position = "dodge")  +
> >     geom_line(aes(group = tsbf)) +
> >     scale_shape_manual(breaks = levels(tmp$tsbf),
> >                        values = 15:17)
>
> > It's hard to distinguish the blue and green colors, so define the

>
> > last_plot() + scale_colour_manual(breaks = levels(tmp$tsbf),
> >                                                   values = c('green',
> > 'blue', 'orange'))
>
> > It's not perfect, but it's an improvement...
>
> > HTH,

#This test results in double the space between the top legend and the graph
test2 <- ggplot(data=PlantGrowth, aes(x=group, y=weight )) + geom_point(aes(colour=group,shape=day))

The upcoming version of ggplot2 has better documentation, contained in the top part of this file:

And if you want to see the code that's actually used to make the models and prediction lines, see here:

-Winston

messages.subject: Log scales (coord_trans) and a regression line (stat_smooth)
messages.subject_clean: Log scales (coord_trans) and a regression line (stat_smooth)
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

## I have a problem of scales which might not be solvable. In a nut
shell, I want to plot two variables where I expect that plotting them
on a log scale will produce a linear relationship. What I am having
trouble doing is plotting a figure with a log scale and a line from a
regression that follows that relationship. I can one or the other but
not both. I've made trivial example (which is I admit a bit
ridiculous) but serve to highlight my problem.

## Need ggplot2 and a dataframe
require(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(x=1:1000,y=log(x), z=c("A","B"))

## So say I have this relationship
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~z)

## And if I plot it on log scales using coord_trans, it a presented with a
## linear trend. But if I try to add a regression line with stat_smooth,
## I am given the regression line of the previous relationship using the
## non-transformed scales. What I am especially after here is those nice\
## log scales on the x axis
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_point()+
  stat_smooth(method="lm") +
  coord_trans(x="log")+
  facet_wrap(~z)

## If I log the actual variable, then the regression is performed on
the right data
## but the x scale is a log scale like the above plot
ggplot(df, aes(x=log(x), y=y)) +
  geom_point()+
  stat_smooth(method="lm") +
  facet_wrap(~z)

## I realized that ggplot2 and R are doing exactly what I am telling
them to do here but I am wondering
## if there is a way to accomplish this plot with log scales and the
post-transformed regression line.

## Thanks in advance!

Sam

messages.body_plain:
I have recently been acquainted ggplot2, which I like very much.

I am producing a plot intended for submission. It’s a 2 by 2 grid of plots written to a pdf file.  To that end I am using the code as explained on page 154 of the ggplot2 book, i.e.,

# this is just test data:

x = 1:20

y = 1 + 2*x+rnorm(20)

mydata = as.data.frame(cbind(x,y))

(a = qplot(x,y,data=mydata, main = "Figure 1(a)", xlab = "Delta", ylab = "Relative MSE") )

(b = qplot(x,y,data=mydata, main = "Figure 1(b)", xlab = "Delta", ylab = "Relative MSE") )

(c = qplot(x,y,data=mydata,main = "Figure 1(c)", xlab = "Delta", ylab = "Relative MSE") )

(d =qplot(x,y,data=mydata,main = "Figure 1(d)", xlab = "Delta", ylab = "Relative MSE") )

pdf("Figure1.pdf", width = 8, height =8, title = This is Figure 1")

grid.newpage()

pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(2,2)))

vplayout = function(x,y)

viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)

print(a,vp = vplayout(1,1))

print(b,vp = vplayout(1,2))

print(c,vp = vplayout(2,1))

print(d,vp = vplayout(2,2))

dev.off()

I would like also to add a main title to the page. How is that done?

Thanks for your help,

Ori

Ori Davidov

Department of Statistics

Univesity of Haifa

messages.subject: the colour about qplot
messages.subject_clean: the colour about qplot
messages.body_plain:
hello all,

I'm reading the book ggplot2 Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis. in the  page 22, the command

qplot(unemploy / pop, uempmed, data = economics,
geom = "path", colour = year(date)) + scale_area()

plot the right figure.

I wonder why there are four colours and four legends.

if I use the following commands

set.seed(1410) # Make the sample reproducible
dsmall <- economics[sample(nrow(economics), 100), ]
year <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$year + 1900
qplot(unemploy / pop, uempmed, data = dsmall,
  geom = "path", colour = year(date)) + scale_area()

there are eight colours and four legends.

what is the mechanism of the colour option? why sometimes four sometimes eight?

thanks in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Were any changes made to the implementation of alpha blending in
ggplot2? Usually, I can load ggplot2, and add alpha blending to a plot
via:

> x=rnorm(10000)
> y=rnorm(10000)
> plot(x,y,pch=19,col=alpha("black",0.33))
Error in plot.xy(xy, type, ...) : could not find function "alpha"

However, this command doesn't seem to be working anymore. Any help
would be great!

messages.body_plain:
Hi, GgploteRs,

I'm trying to create a barchart that has both dodged and stacked components. Here's an example, which gets the picture somewhat right:

library(ggplot2)
my.data <- data.frame(A = c("incr", "incr", "decr", "decr", "incr", "incr", "decr", "decr"),
                      B = c("lots", "some", "some", "lots", "lots", "some", "some", "lots"),
                      C = c("g1", "g1", "g1", "g1", "g2", "g2", "g2", "g2"),
                      value = c(0.1, 0.2, -0.1, -0.2, 0.05, 0.1, -0.05, -0.01))
my.data$BA <- paste(my.data$B, my.data$A)
my.data$AC <- paste(my.data$A, my.data$C)
my.data$BA <- factor(my.data$BA, unique(my.data$BA))
my.data$AC <- factor(my.data$AC, unique(my.data$AC))

gg <- ggplot(my.data, aes(AC, value))
gg <- gg + geom_bar(aes(fill = BA), stat = "identity")
gg <- gg + labs(fill = "")
gg <- gg + scale_x_discrete("", breaks = c(1.5, 3.5),
                            labels = levels(my.data$C))
gg <- gg + scale_y_continuous("", formatter = "percent")
gg

A few of questions:
1. Is there a better way of doing this? Currently I have to create the column AC, which I think is suboptimal. My method produces equal spacing across all 4 levels of AC. Ideally, I would like the child groups of AC ("incr", "decr") to be closer together than the parent groups ("g1", "g2").
2. Is the "breaks" argument in scale_x_discrete ignored, or am I choosing the wrong breaks? I'd like to have only two tick marks for the two levels C rather than the 4 tick marks for the four levels of AC.
3. The positive stacks are ordered from bottom to top (i.e. "lots incr" below "some incr") while the legend has these in reversed order. The colors are correct, just not the order I want. How can I change this?

messages.body_plain:
Here's a version that works with the current development version:

library(ggplot2)
library(proto)

GeomSegment2 <- proto(ggplot2:::GeomSegment, {
 objname <- "geom_segment2"

 draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, arrow=NULL, ...) {

   if (is.linear(coordinates)) {
     return(with(coord_transform(coordinates, data, scales),

       segmentsGrob(x, y, xend, yend, default.units="native",
       gp = gpar(col=alpha(colour, alpha), lwd=size * .pt,
         lty=linetype, lineend = "round"),
       arrow = arrow)
     ))
   }

}})

geom_segment2 <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL, stat =
"identity", position = "identity", arrow = NULL, ...)  {
  GeomSegment2$new(mapping = mapping, data = data, stat = stat,
        position = position, arrow = arrow, ...)
}
df <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1)
ggplot(df, aes(x , y)) + geom_segment2(aes(xend = x + 1, yend = y +
1), size = 4)
ggplot(df, aes(x , y)) + geom_segment(aes(xend = x + 1, yend = y + 1), size = 4)

I think the main problem with your code was that you were inheriting
from Geom instead of GeomSegment, and so your custom geom was missing
many important functions.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Sundar,

Generally you're going to have to calculate your own offsets when trying
 to manually specify where you want to place items.  Essentially, you're
 going to have to artificially make your child groups closer together on
 the x-axis.  You might find that splitting your AC column into two
columns and separating the factors to be useful.  That way you could
calculate the x-axis values in such a way as to control the grouping.

aes(x=parentAC+childAC, y=value) #where the value of the main grouping
column is 5 or 10 and the secondary grouping is a smaller value like 1 or 2.

So if you wanted the child columns to be closer together, have childAC be the main grouping value.

e.g.
gg <- ggplot(my.data, aes(x=as.numeric(A)*5+as.numeric(C), value))

gg <- gg + geom_bar(aes(fill = BA), stat = "identity")
gg <- gg + labs(fill = "")

gg <- gg + scale_x_discrete( labels = levels(my.data$C))
gg <- gg + scale_y_continuous( formatter = "percent")
gg

Then simply assign breaks and labels as you see fit.

Hi Juliet:

This isn't perfect, but it's reasonably close. The first problem you
had was to use a weight aesthetic - no such thing exists in ggplot2
AFAIK. What you wanted, I think, was 'stat = identity' to be set in
geom_bar().

I had some difficulty getting the order of the bars to match up
exactly, but what I have is rather close. I didn't use the brewer
palette, but defined my own discrete color set instead; for some
reason, it seems to want to map greyscales to white in the plot and
legend. Changing it to 'grey20', a much darker grey shade, made no
difference. This is the same kind of problem you reported and I don't
have a good answer for you.  All of the grayxx and greyxx shades are
in colors(), but they don't show up when defined as a value of a
color/colour aesthetic. Perhaps the greyscale colors are reserved for
scale_grey() in ggplot2, but Hadley is in a better position to answer
whether or not that's the case.

I found it easier to divide the melted data frame into two: one for
the disagree categories, where I assigned values to be non-positive,
and the other for the neutral-agree categories, where the values are
positive. My initial plot with the entire melted data frame didn't
respect the zero line properly. Another change I made was to shorten
the length of the category labels by inserting \n in a few places. The
0.8.9 version plot isn't quite as nice because the legend at the
bottom gets cut off on each edge; a more flexible one is shown in the
development version 0.9.0. See the attachments to compare the two.

Pardon that I changed all of the data frame names - I went out and
tried to do this on my own from scratch based on the HH plot and
looked at your code a bit later. We both did pretty much the same
thing, though :)

Starting from the data object in HH,

DF <- as.data.frame(ProfChal[[2]])
DF[['Category']] <- rownames(DF)
DF$Category[3] <- 'Federal, state and\nlocal government'
DF$Category[4] <- 'Private consultant/\nself-employed'
DF$Category[5] <- 'Other (including retired, \nstudents, not employed, etc.)'
DF[['Strongly Disagree']] <-   -DF[['Strongly Disagree']]
DF[['Disagree']] <-   -DF[['Disagree']]

library('reshape2')
dfm <- melt(DF, id = 'Category')
dfmpos <- subset(dfm, value > 0)
dfmneg <- subset(dfm, value <= 0)

# 0.8.9 plot  (legend not quite so nice, but it helped to break up the
category labels)
ggplot(dfmpos, aes(x = Category, y = value, fill = variable)) +
    theme_bw() +
    geom_bar(stat = 'identity', position = 'stack') +
    geom_bar(data = dfmneg, stat = 'identity', position = 'stack') +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c('Strongly Disagree' = 'red',
'Disagree' = 'orange',
                                 'No opinion' = 'gray90', 'Agree' = 'lightblue',
                                 'Strongly Agree' = 'blue')) +
    labs(y = 'Count', x = '', fill = 'Response') +
    opts(legend.position = 'bottom',
         title = 'Do you find your job challenging?',
         axis.x.text = theme_text(size = 8)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = 'grey65') +
    coord_flip()

# 0.9.0 plot (use guide_legend() to modify certain features
#                 of the legend)
ggplot(dfmpos, aes(x = Category, y = value, fill = variable)) +
    theme_bw() +
    geom_bar(stat = 'identity', position = 'stack') +
    geom_bar(data = dfmneg, stat = 'identity', position = 'stack') +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, direction = 'horizontal',
                               label.theme = theme_text(size = 8))) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c('Strongly Disagree' = 'red',
'Disagree' = 'orange',
                                 'No opinion' = 'gray90', 'Agree' = 'lightblue',
                                 'Strongly Agree' = 'blue')) +
    labs(y = 'Count', x = '', fill = 'Response') +
    opts(legend.position = 'bottom',
         title = 'Do you find your job challenging?',
         axis.x.text = theme_text(size = 8)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = 'grey65') +
    coord_flip()

If you haven't tried the new version yet, here's how to download it.
Preferably in a fresh R session,

library('devtools')
dev_mode()       # should reply 'dev_mode ON'
install_github('ggplot2')   # wait a little for it to install
library('ggplot2')

Then reload the data and try the second ggplot() call.

Hope this is of some help,
Dennis

almost always too far away), to the point where they sometimes overlap
labels depending on the exact plot size.  I figured I could use the
'vjust' parameter to adjust this, but it looks like the text gets
clipped (!)

I'm just confusing myself) that the 4th element in the margin vector
controls the left-hand margin (in base R this would be the 2d element in

messages.body_plain:
Me again.

  Still using ggplot 0.9.0.  I would try reverting to ggplot 0.8.9 to
see if these are new bugs or if I'm just doing something boneheaded, but
it seems like too much of a nuisance (sorry).  Perhaps someone can
confirm whether these work in 0.8.9.

  Two issues:

 (1) stat_sum() seems to ignore the colour aesthetic ... ?
 (2) when I facet_grid I seem to lose the desired behavio(u)r of
stat_sum.  This is probably something silly, but I have tried
experimenting with setting the group aesthetic manually and don't seem
to have found a combination that works.

set.seed(101)
d <- data.frame(x=sample(1:5,size=500,replace=TRUE),
                y=sample(1:5,size=500,replace=TRUE),
                g=sample(c("a","b"),size=500,replace=TRUE))

## creates coloured points
ggplot(d,aes(x,y,colour=g))+geom_point()+facet_grid(.~g)

## no colour -- also no distinctive sizes
ggplot(d,aes(x,y,colour=g))+
  stat_sum(aes(group=interaction(x,y,g)))+facet_grid(.~g)

## this works as expected (no colour, different sizes)
ggplot(d,aes(x=x,y=y))+stat_sum()

## aiming for something that looks like this:
library(reshape2)
mm <- melt(with(d,table(x,y,g)))
ggplot(mm,aes(x=x,y=y,colour=g))+geom_point(aes(size=value))+
  facet_grid(.~g)

 thanks
   Ben Bolker

messages.subject: Re: ggplot figure tweaking/clipping
messages.subject_clean: ggplot figure tweaking/clipping
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben:

vjust = 0.32 looked reasonable to me after some trial and error.

The title spacing problem was fixed in 0.9.0, but of course that was
for the default font sizes. When the titles and axis labels are
magnified, all bets are off. I'm wondering if there's a way to code
themes so that when the font sizes are increased by a certain
magnitude, the plot background area is increased proportionally to
accommodate them. I'm not familiar enough with the code to know how
easy or hard that would be to do, though.

I played around with plot.margin = a little bit; all it does is pad
the total graphics region with white space. Play around with the
parameters and you'll find that it affects the size of the graph in
the document, shrinking it to accommodate the outside padding, but
doesn't really affect the rendering of the graph per se. Even with all
plot margins zero the y-axis title was still clipped at vjust = 0.25.
I think the relevant parameter in this problem is vjust because of the
size of the font.

Side note: knitr will save plots created within the document in the
same directory where the .Rnw file resides. If you want saved 7 x 7
plots, you should make fig.width and fig.height = 7 in the
\SweaveOpts{} chunk. It's also worth naming the code chunks because
the graphs will get saved with the name of the chunk. [chunk-name.dev <http://chunk-name.dev>,
where dev is the device specified.] In addition, you don't need
fig=TRUE in version 0.2; the argument has been deprecated and replaced
by fig.show and fig.keep. See the most recent documentation at the
knitr web site for details.

The document of mine to which Brandon referred doesn't use plot.margin
= anywhere, so that won't be of any help wrt this problem...but thanks
for the mention, Brandon :)

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dennis,

Thanks for your help. You tuned my eye to a different aspect of the
plot that I had missed. The bars are centered at the middle
category. I'm still thinking about if this improves the plot or not.
I'll build off what you did to decide. Any thoughts?

As for the colors, the following helped with my original attempt.

p <- p + scale_fill_manual(values=c("#CA0020", "#F4A582", "gray90",
"#92C5DE", "#0571B0"))

Juliet

On Mon, Jan 30, 2012 at 6:37 PM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Juliet:
>
> This isn't perfect, but it's reasonably close. The first problem you
> had was to use a weight aesthetic - no such thing exists in ggplot2
> AFAIK. What you wanted, I think, was 'stat = identity' to be set in
> geom_bar().
>
> I had some difficulty getting the order of the bars to match up
> exactly, but what I have is rather close. I didn't use the brewer
> palette, but defined my own discrete color set instead; for some
> reason, it seems to want to map greyscales to white in the plot and
> legend. Changing it to 'grey20', a much darker grey shade, made no
> difference. This is the same kind of problem you reported and I don't
> have a good answer for you.  All of the grayxx and greyxx shades are
> in colors(), but they don't show up when defined as a value of a
> color/colour aesthetic. Perhaps the greyscale colors are reserved for
> scale_grey() in ggplot2, but Hadley is in a better position to answer
> whether or not that's the case.
>
> I found it easier to divide the melted data frame into two: one for
> the disagree categories, where I assigned values to be non-positive,
> and the other for the neutral-agree categories, where the values are
> positive. My initial plot with the entire melted data frame didn't
> respect the zero line properly. Another change I made was to shorten
> the length of the category labels by inserting \n in a few places. The
> 0.8.9 version plot isn't quite as nice because the legend at the
> bottom gets cut off on each edge; a more flexible one is shown in the
> development version 0.9.0. See the attachments to compare the two.
>
> Pardon that I changed all of the data frame names - I went out and
> tried to do this on my own from scratch based on the HH plot and
> looked at your code a bit later. We both did pretty much the same
> thing, though :)
>
> Starting from the data object in HH,
>
> DF <- as.data.frame(ProfChal[[2]])
> DF[['Category']] <- rownames(DF)
> DF$Category[3] <- 'Federal, state and\nlocal government'
> DF$Category[4] <- 'Private consultant/\nself-employed'
> DF$Category[5] <- 'Other (including retired, \nstudents, not employed, etc.)'
> DF[['Strongly Disagree']] <-   -DF[['Strongly Disagree']]
> DF[['Disagree']] <-   -DF[['Disagree']]
>
> library('reshape2')
> dfm <- melt(DF, id = 'Category')
> dfmpos <- subset(dfm, value > 0)
> dfmneg <- subset(dfm, value <= 0)
>
> # 0.8.9 plot  (legend not quite so nice, but it helped to break up the
> category labels)
> ggplot(dfmpos, aes(x = Category, y = value, fill = variable)) +
>    theme_bw() +
>    geom_bar(stat = 'identity', position = 'stack') +
>    geom_bar(data = dfmneg, stat = 'identity', position = 'stack') +
>    scale_fill_manual(values = c('Strongly Disagree' = 'red',
> 'Disagree' = 'orange',
>                                 'No opinion' = 'gray90', 'Agree' = 'lightblue',
>                                 'Strongly Agree' = 'blue')) +
>    labs(y = 'Count', x = '', fill = 'Response') +
>    opts(legend.position = 'bottom',
>         title = 'Do you find your job challenging?',
>         axis.x.text = theme_text(size = 8)) +
>    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = 'grey65') +
>    coord_flip()
>
> # 0.9.0 plot (use guide_legend() to modify certain features
> #                 of the legend)
> ggplot(dfmpos, aes(x = Category, y = value, fill = variable)) +
>    theme_bw() +
>    geom_bar(stat = 'identity', position = 'stack') +
>    geom_bar(data = dfmneg, stat = 'identity', position = 'stack') +
>    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, direction = 'horizontal',
>                               label.theme = theme_text(size = 8))) +
>    scale_fill_manual(values = c('Strongly Disagree' = 'red',
> 'Disagree' = 'orange',
>                                 'No opinion' = 'gray90', 'Agree' = 'lightblue',
>                                 'Strongly Agree' = 'blue')) +
>    labs(y = 'Count', x = '', fill = 'Response') +
>    opts(legend.position = 'bottom',
>         title = 'Do you find your job challenging?',
>         axis.x.text = theme_text(size = 8)) +
>    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = 'grey65') +
>    coord_flip()
>
>
> If you haven't tried the new version yet, here's how to download it.
> Preferably in a fresh R session,
>
> library('devtools')
> dev_mode()       # should reply 'dev_mode ON'
> install_github('ggplot2')   # wait a little for it to install
> library('ggplot2')
>
> Then reload the data and try the second ggplot() call.
>
> Hope this is of some help,
> Dennis
>
> On Mon, Jan 30, 2012 at 12:43 PM, Juliet Hannah <juliet...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> All,
>>
>> I am trying to reproduce a plot from the hh library. Here is the
>> example from ?plot.likert.
>>
>>
>> library("HH")
>>
>> data(ProfChal)  ## List of named matrices.  See below for discussion
>> of the dataset.
>> ProfChal[[2]]
>>
>> ## Count plot
>> plot.likert(ProfChal[[2]],
>>            main='Is your job professionally challenging?',
>>            sub="This plot looks better in a 9in x 4in window.")
>>
>> Here is my ggplot2 version:
>>
>>
>> library("reshape")
>> library("ggplot2")
>>
>> myData <- ProfChal[[2]]
>> myData <- data.frame(myData)
>> myData$type <- rownames(myData)
>> rownames(myData) <- NULL
>>
>> mData <- melt(myData, id="type")
>> mData$variable <-
>> factor(mData$variable,levels=c("Strongly.Disagree","Disagree","No.Opinion","Agree","Strongly.Agree"))
>> mData$type <- factor(mData$type)
>> mData$type <- factor(mData$type,levels=rev(levels(mData$type)))
>>
>>
>> p <- ggplot(mData,aes(x=type,weight=value))
>> p <- p + geom_bar(aes(fill=variable))
>> p <- p + scale_fill_brewer(pal="RdBu")
>> p <- p + coord_flip()
>> p <- p + theme_bw()
>>
>>
>> In my version, the middle color is white. The source code for
>> plot.likert has the following note and modification. Note how it sets
>> the middle color.
>>
>>
>>                                BrewerPaletteName="RdBu",
>>                                ## These are the diverging palettes in
>> RColorBrewer
>>                                ## c("RdBu", "BrBG", "PiYG", "PRGn", "PuOr",
>>                                ## "RdGy", "RdYlBu", "RdYlGn", "Spectral"),
>>                                reference.line.col="gray65",

>> is the RColorBrewer default for middle.color in the RdBu scheme
>>                                col.strip.background="gray97",
>>                                col=brewer.pal.likert(attr(x,
>> "nlevels"), BrewerPaletteName, middle.color),

>> How can I modify my ggplot2 syntax to mimic this behavior?

messages.subject: Re: printing labels along lines
messages.subject_clean: printing labels along lines
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's a way to get something close to your first graph in version 0.8.9:

d <- data.frame(mon = seq(as.Date('2010-09-01'),
as.Date('2011-05-01'), by = '1 month'),
                y1 = c(9, 10, 9, 11, 10, 11, 10, 9, 9),
                y2 = c(17, 14, 16, 15, 14, 15, 16, 17, 17))
as.numeric(d$mon)

lab1 <- 'First multi-line\nchart annotation'
lab2 <- 'Second multi-line\nchart annotation'

ggplot(d, aes(x = mon)) +
    theme_bw() +
    geom_rect(xmin = 14000, xmax = 16000, ymin = 10, ymax = 30, fill =
'ivory') +
    geom_line(aes(y = y1), colour = 'red', linetype = 'dashed', size = 1) +
    geom_line(aes(y = y2), colour = 'gold', size = 1) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 14900, y = 17.5, label = lab1)) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 14950, y = 12.5, label = lab2)) +
    ylim(0, 20) +
    scale_x_date(major = '1 month', format = '%b') +
    opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
         panel.grid.minor = theme_blank()) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = seq(0, 20, by = 2.5)), colour = 'grey80')

A few comments:

(1) The main problem is that the x-axis is plotting dates, but both
geom_rect() and geom_text() need numeric coordinates for correct
positioning. It took a few minutes to figure this out, but you need to
use the numeric values of the dates in order for geom_text() and
geom_rect() to work.
(2) You can use \n inside a text string to break a line. I created two
text strings with an embedded \n, lab1 and lab2, and then passed them
in separate geom_text() calls.
(3) If you want a (partially) color filled background in the graphics
region, it's best to call geom_rect() before any other geom so that
the background is rendered first. That's why geom_rect() was first in
line in my call.
(4) A small modification to the code works in the latest version of 0.9.0:

library('scales')    # needed for the scale_x_date() call
ggplot(d, aes(x = mon)) +
    theme_bw() +
    geom_rect(xmin = 14000, xmax = 16000, ymin = 10, ymax = 30, fill =
'ivory') +
    geom_line(aes(y = y1), colour = 'red', linetype = 'dashed', size = 1) +
    geom_line(aes(y = y2), colour = 'gold', size = 1) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 14900, y = 17.5, label = lab1)) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 14950, y = 12.5, label = lab2)) +
    ylim(0, 20) +
    scale_x_date(breaks = date_breaks('1 month'),
                 labels = date_format('%b')) +
    opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
         panel.grid.minor = theme_blank()) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = seq(0, 20, by = 2.5)), colour = 'grey80')

Until recently, there was a bug in geom_hline() and geom_vline() in
the development version that threw an error (which I discovered in a
session that did not have the latest GitHub installation).

HTH,
Dennis
